title: Jensen Huang Is Out at Nvidia
author: Max Read, Whitney Jones, Vjeran Pavic, Daniel Ramirez, Dan Powell, Marion Lozano and Rowan Niemisto
text:
Original music by Dan Powell Marion Lozano and Rowan Niemisto

Jensen Huang is out as chief executive of Nvidia. It’s a stunning fall for one the most powerful figures of the A.I. boom.

To make sense of it all, we’re joined by two of the reporters who’ve been leading the coverage for The New York Times, Ana Swanson and Ryan Mac, alongside Stephen Witt, the author of the Jensen Huang biography “The Thinking Machine.”

We’ll discuss how we got here, the significance of a Jensen-less Nvidia and what happens next.

title: Who Could Replace Jensen Huang as Nvidia’s CEO? Here Are 7 Candidates.
author: Don Clark
text:
Finding a successor to Jensen Huang at Nvidia is being compared to replacing Steve Jobs at Apple. In many ways, it’s actually harder.

Mr. Huang, 63, has much deeper technical expertise than the late Mr. Jobs did, with a keen understanding of the field of artificial intelligence and what chips and other technologies are needed to support it.

Unlike Mr. Jobs, Mr. Huang also forged close friendships throughout the industry, creating a complex network of partners, customers and suppliers. He turned Nvidia into a major player in Washington, built on a close relationship with President Trump and technology vital to U.S. national security.

And Mr. Huang shaped a culture at Nvidia that drove rapid-fire innovation while attracting some of the most accomplished engineers.

“They have to get someone who is an inspirational leader, that people love,” said Jeff Christian, chief executive of Christian & Timbers, an executive recruiting firm that frequently works with Silicon Valley companies. “This person has to be a great talent engineer, and a great talent magnet.”

Any candidate would also need an impeccable record for integrity and honesty, Mr. Christian and others noted.

title: In reversal, American Cancer Society urges routine prostate cancer screening
author: Beth Mole
text:
In a significant update to its guidelines for prostate cancer screening, the American Cancer Society is now recommending that men get routinely screened for prostate cancer with a PSA (prostate-specific antigen) test.

Men considered at high risk due to race and family history should start testing earlier, at 45, and most are recommended to get tested every year. Specifically, yearly testing starting at age 45 is recommended for all Black men, who have higher rates of prostate cancer. Non-Black men should also get yearly testing starting at 45 if a close relative was diagnosed with prostate cancer before age 65, or if more than one of their relatives has had prostate cancer. On the other hand, if only one close relative was diagnosed with prostate cancer and it was diagnosed at age 65 or older, non-Black men in this case should start PSA screening at 45, but are recommended to get testing only every two years.

title: Some under-25s should get fewer benefits, Milburn review to say
text:
Some young people could see reductions to the benefits they are entitled to, under a radical overhaul of the system to be recommended by a government-commissioned review.

Alan Milburn's year-long report, which will be published on Tuesday, will recommend moving under-25s off the main sickness and disability benefits, the Times reported , external .

Milburn, a former Labour health secretary, has been tasked by the government with helping reduce the one in eight 18- to 24-year-olds in the UK who are not in education, employment or training - or "Neet".

He said on Wednesday night that his plans would not be "pain-free" and would affect both existing and new claimants.

His report is expected to recommend that under-25s are no longer able to claim the health element of universal credit or personal independence payment (Pip).

Instead, they would receive an allowance on the same basic rate as universal credit.

Some could be eligible for a new "additional cost allowance" to cover day-to-day costs related to their conditions.

But many claimants would receive less under the plans, which the government is set to take forward into legislation in the new year.

Milburn, a Labour MP from 1992 to 2010, is also expected to recommend an investment of billions into more employment support for young people, including work placements, job subsidies and one-to-one personal advisers.

Those with more severe disabilities and unable to work would get a new benefit paid at a higher rate.

Speaking to the Times about his report, Milburn said: "Candidly, it could mean that some people will get less financial support at the beginning of their benefit claim than under the current system.

"But actually, for young people, there's a different debate that we've got to resolve, which is whether the priority is their longer-term life chances or just their immediate shorter-term finances.

"I think what the current system does [is] it prioritises the latter over the former. I believe that's the wrong choice and it needs to be the other way around."

Just under one million young people in the UK are Neets , data from the Office for National Statistics (ONS) from April to June suggests. This was a rise of 3% on the same period last year.

Milburn's recommendations are likely to be backed by Prime Minister Andy Burnham but could prove controversial among Labour MPs, who opposed welfare reform under his predecessor Sir Keir Starmer.

The reforms would represent a radical overhaul of Britain's welfare system, at a time when there is heavy political pressure for the UK to find the money to spend more on defence.

If Milburn's recommendations were approved, it could take almost a decade for the British state to see monetary savings.

The new system "will need significant investment" and would involve "rebuilding the system from scratch," Milburn added.

He said that currently "you've got hundreds of thousands of young people stuck in a benefit system that is trapping them in poverty, giving them no prospect of prosperity or a job".

His new proposed system would involve an element of carrot and stick, where young people could lose some of their benefits if they did not engage with the extra work support options.

"A deal isn't a deal unless there are potential consequences," Milburn said. "Entitlements and responsibilities are two sides of the same coin."

A government spokesperson said: "We will always ensure there is a safety net for the most vulnerable and those who are unable to work.

"But the prime minister has been clear that we need a wholesale change in the way we support young people to grow up in this country, where we invest in their success rather than paying for failure."

title: You Don’t Have to Like 32s, But That Doesn’t Mean You’re Right
author: Logan Jones-Wilkins
text:
I am going to lead with this at the top: this article is going to make a lot of people mad. I have seen the comments, the skepticism, the what-about-ery.

All of that is to say, forget your feelings . Thirty-two-inch gravel bikes make riding gravel so much more fun.

Up until this point, I have tried to remain neutral and objective. I have reported on 32-inch gravel tech since Sea Otter, and throughout that coverage I have couched my position in caveats, qualifiers, and fence-sitting.

I am not doing that anymore. After riding the Mosaic GT i55 32 gravel bike, I can say with clear eyes and a good conscience that all you haters are plain wrong. The bike is not perfect, but it is a phenomenal representation that the vast majority of 32-inch criticism is just not valid.

After hundreds of miles of riding across as many surfaces as I could find, the new wheels have clicked for me emphatically, and not for the way you might think. Speed, while top of mind in many of the 32-inch discussions, wasn’t the point that got me. It might have been faster, but ultimately that was less important than the other pull.

On gravel, the bike just cruises; that’s the only way I can distill it. It’s a dreamboat, holding traction well beyond smaller tires of similar tread and width, and carries so much speed every time it goes downhill. While I wasn’t at the front of the Big Sugar peloton, there were only one or two instances out of the 50 miles of racing where anyone could match the speed on downhills.

From a mix of a stable platform for pedaling through chunky terrain and preserving inertia through loose turns, I was constantly catching and passing people every time the road would tilt down, or the track got rough.

It was emphatically good at doing the things that smart people in the industry have been saying it would be well suited for.

Yeah, what about that handling! The 32-inch bike handled better than the vast majority of gravel bikes I have ridden, across the board. Sweeping bends? Yup. Chunky two-track? Absolutely. Twisty single track? Yes, with a bullet.

What the Mosaic 32 proved to me was how many people’s consideration of what makes good gravel bike handling is based around a deeply flawed premise. Largely, many bike riders think bikes with shorter wheelbases and steep angles have better handling, and long-wheelbase bikes are sluggish and cumbersome. In some circumstances, this might be true, but for any stretch of the definition of gravel racing, this paradigm is almost completely backwards.

Shorter geometry on gravel bikes does not make them turn better, accelerate faster, or handle more reliably. As long as the bike has balance, it can be long as hell and feel much, much more nimble.

There is a path for gravel bike design to have its cake and eat it, too. Current options with big tires and short chainstays, however, are like eating a bowl of frosting. Some might like it, but most would actually prefer the cake.

Ultimately, the myth about shorter chainstays helping handling runs so deep it is hard to push back on. It is a crowded hill that some of the biggest bike brands in the world seem set to die on. Yet, in short, shorter chainstays are susceptible to understeer. Understeer is what happens when a bike’s rear wheel tracks tighter around a corner than the front.

It is also the cause of most crashes that involve the front wheel slipping out or a rider blasting through the exit of a turn.

Another way of putting it is that understeer makes the rear wheel go straight when the front wheel is turning.

On mountain bikes, when the speeds are low and the turns are super tight, the longer wheelbase can backfire. But on gravel at speed, the longer wheelbase and chainstay will result in a much more rounded rear wheel trajectory and, ultimately, the ability to take more aggressive lines and speeds through cornering.

Thirty-two-inch wheels force bikes to have much longer chainstays. That is the underlying variable that immediately jumped out as I rode the bike. Even with the bigger wheels, it handled terrain better, even tight, twisty terrain the critics think would be the death of it.

Add in the better traction, increased stability, and quick front-end handling of a relatively steeper head tube angle, and the Mosaic 32 didn’t feel much different from some of my favorite 29-inch gravel bikes that pushed their rear ends to the appropriate length—it just held traction for a bit longer and rolled down hills just a bit faster.

As I mentioned, the Mosaic is not perfect. Thirty-two-inch wheels as a whole are not perfect. On road, the system is unequivocally slower. The weight, aero losses, and added height of the system are all things that outpace the rolling benefit on tarmac.

The weight is also unavoidable. Thirty-two-inch bikes are just bigger. There is just more material, and stiffness is harder to engineer around. It will always be a weight penalty, and that will make a difference on many routes. For Big Sugar, the rolling nature of the course made the 32 easily the better option for most riders. But for gravel rides with more sustained climbing and less gravel, the 21-pound build of the titanium 32-inch bike might be a slower overall option compared to a 17-pound 29-inch gravel bike.

I think because of these two aspects that won’t necessarily change in the big wheels’ favor, 29-inch will stick around, as there could easily be demand for both depending on what the consumer is looking for.

Speaking of consumers, the other fundamental criticism of 32-inch gravel bikes is how the bikes will scale down to smaller riders. While some of this concern is justified, I do think the prospect of 32-inch gravel for short riders is much better than for mountain biking.…

title: Donald Trump Jr exits as paid adviser for prediction market Kalshi
author: Associated Press
text:
Kalshi announces ‘mutual decision’ as Democrats say they plan to investigate Trump family’s investments

Donald Trump Jr is no longer a paid adviser for Kalshi, the prediction market company said Thursday.

Kalshi described it as a mutual business decision between the two parties that followed a decision by Trump Jr’s investment firm, 1789 Capital, to increase its investment in Kalshi’s biggest competitor Polymarket.

But the announcement comes a week after Democrats were able to take control of both the House and Senate in the midterm elections.

Democrats have said they planned to investigate the Trump family’s investments, including their business relationships with both prediction markets.

“We have mutually agreed to end Don’s advisory role after his firm’s significant investment in a competitor this past summer,” said Dani Lever, a spokesperson for Kalshi. “We are grateful for his contributions in helping us market Kalshi to more customers.”

The president’s eldest son became a paid “strategic adviser” for Kalshi shortly after President Trump was sworn into office for his second term in January 2025 and has been an investor in Polymarket since August 2025. Both companies have seen their popularity and use jump significantly in the past two years.

At the same time, both companies have received favorable treatment from the White House. The Commodity Futures Trading Commission has backed the industry’s efforts to expand their products nationwide, including allowing their customers to trade sports-related contracts.

Both companies have adamantly denied that the financial relationship between Polymarket, Kalshi and the Trumps played any role in how the industry has been regulated under this administration.

1789 Capital increased its investment in Polymarket this past August, as part of Polymarket’s latest fundraising round. It was this investment that started the conversation about ending Trump Jr’s advisory role with Kalshi.

title: ‘Win-win’ deal with EU could be done, Andy Burnham says
author: Jennifer Rankin in Dublin, Jessica Elgot, Lisa O’Carroll and Pippa Crerar
text:
Prime minister says reset could be a deal ‘like the Brexit people thought they were voting for in 2016’

Andy Burnham has said he believes a “win-win” deal could be done with the EU that could be “more like the Brexit that people thought they were voting for in 2016”.

The prime minister was meeting fellow leaders at the European Political Community summit in Dublin, ahead of a keenly anticipated EU-UK summit next week, where he hopes to bring Britain closer to Europe .

At the bilateral summit the EU and UK hope to sign deals on food and drink, emissions trading and a youth mobility scheme, but the question of tuition fees for European students remains a stumbling block.

Burnham said: “I believe there is a good deal to be done that could be a win-win for Britain and Europe.

“The deal is not done, and there’ll be some long nights ahead in the next seven days.”

He said the reset would be about whether we can “take a step back to closer working relationships with Europe”.

Burnham added: “We ended up with a far harder Brexit , I think, than people thought they were getting when they went to the polls.”

The EU has said the prized food and drink deal and emissions-trading agreement may not enter into force without a deal on tuition fees in which European students would pay domestic rates.

Burnham said it was a package deal, but would not be drawn on whether he accepted the link. “I’m going to be fighting hard for these benefits for Britain in the next seven days … they will make a real difference. If I can do anything to address the cost of living crisis, I should be doing it.”

He has previously said the food and drink deal, which will ease Brexit red tape, will add 0.4% to British GDP.

The prime minister also said David Cameron had been wrong to argue that Britain’s problems had “nothing to do with Brexit”, adding there would be “long nights ahead” to negotiate a reset with the EU before the summit.

Cameron, the prime minister who lost the 2016 Brexit referendum, told Bloomberg News that Burnham should not seek to bring Britain back into the EU, arguing that the UK’s problems had nothing to do with its exit from the EU.

Asked about those remarks, Burnham said: “I think he is wrong to say that the low growth that we’ve had over the last decade has, quote, ‘nothing to do with Brexit’. I would say the evidence says otherwise.

“It feels like his intervention is more about unity in the Conservative party than it is about fighting for the British interests.”

Burnham has recently said he is open to rejoining the single market, customs union or to “go all the way” by rejoining the EU. He said a deeper relationship would be the outcome of future talks “and it will be in the outcome of that negotiation that then we will take a decision as a cabinet, on what, if anything, comes next”.

Earlier on Thursday, the EU foreign policy chief, Kaja Kallas, said she wanted to see Britain rejoin the EU, but warned that negotiations would not be easy after the “trauma” of the Brexit years.

She said: “I would very much like to see Britain back in Europe, but, of course, we also have in the European Union , a lot of, I would say, trauma from Britain leaving, so the negotiations will not be that easy.”

Burnham is expected to make the EU reset the centrepiece of his white-tie speech at the lord mayor’s banquet on Monday night – though it will range widely across foreign policy challenges.

No 10 sources said the speech would be focused on the upcoming Brussels summit – and look ahead to the next stage in 2027 – rather than outline what a more permanent close relationship might look like.

Officials at the UK-EU summit will also discuss the agenda for the next round of the reset, expected to focus on a joint migration pact.

It could also target collaboration on law enforcement and borders, visas for touring artists, and mutual recognition of qualifications.

Ministry of Justice officials are also trying to water down an EU ultimatum on halting the deportation of foreign national offenders. “This is the classic wheeze that the EU always pulls at the last minute of negotiations,” one Whitehall source said.

The next week is expected to be fraught with last-minute negotiations. Key will be access to Made in Europe, which has the potential to lock British firms out of continental supply chains and public contracts if no deal is done.

Negotiations could be challenging despite the lure of the UK making a potential concession on tuition fees in exchange for inclusion in the Made in Europe legislation .

The EU has long said there cannot be a deal on Made in Europe at the summit, because it has yet to finalise its own position.

The joint communique for 2027 is expected to call for strengthening efforts between the UK and the most exposed member states to the small boats crisis in the Channel.

This will centre on both the EU’s Channel action plan, already in place since June this year, and a possible framework for a wider bespoke EU-UK migration plan.

The UK is believed to be pushing for access to the Eurodac database, which carries the fingerprints of asylum seekers, as well as to the Schengen Information System (SIS), which records details on fugitives, missing people and stolen goods.

The UK was the third biggest user of SIS before it lost access through Brexit.

title: China rules out hosting Cop33 climate summit in 2028
author: Fiona Harvey in Antalya
text:
Decision disappoints experts hoping for world’s biggest emitter to take global lead on climate crisis

China has ruled out hosting the Cop33 UN climate summit in 2028 after months of deliberations, leaving the field open for other Asian countries to hold it, the Guardian understands.

The decision will disappoint many countries and climate experts, who had hoped the world’s biggest emitter would take the lead on the global stage, as the US under Donald Trump has vacated all forms of international cooperation on the climate .

Al Gore, the former US vice-president, was among those left disheartened by the decision. “I would be very much in favour of that idea [of China hosting the summit],” he told the Guardian. “It’s too bad.”

China is in the midst of an economic transformation , from being heavily dependent on coal to becoming an “electro state”. John Kerry, the former US secretary of state, told the Guardian that China was leaving the rest of the world behind in forging and using the low-carbon technologies of the future.

Renewable energy generation capacity has now outstripped coal in China, and its greenhouse gas emissions appear to have declined slightly this year.

Sales of electric vehicles in the country have also taken off, making up nearly two-thirds of the market last month, and China’s clean energy industries drove more than 90% of the country’s investment growth last year .

The rules of the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) mean an Asian country should host in 2028.

Gareth Redmond-King, the international lead at the Energy and Climate Intelligence Unit thinktank, said China’s position as an industrial powerhouse would have made it a formidable contender to hold the summit.

“It would undoubtedly be significant for the world’s biggest emitter and second-biggest economy to host a climate Cop,” he said.

“They’re leading the world on investment, manufacture and deployment of clean energy tech, and their emissions have started to tick down. As a leadership story, China hosting Cop33 would be a big deal.”

It is not clear why China has decided against hosting the conference, but several experts that spoke to the Guardian suggested that the US electoral cycle was likely to have been a factor. The next US presidential election will take place on 7 November 2028, and Cop33 is scheduled for 6 to 17 November that year.

After the strong showing by Democrats in the recent midterm elections, in which voter concern over the climate crisis was thought to be a factor , the Democrats will be hoping to elect a climate-friendly president in 2028. But even if they succeed, Trump will still be in office until the following January.

The US president rejects climate science and withdrew the US from the Paris agreement, and is also withdrawing from its parent treaty, the 1992 UNFCCC.

China seeks to be seen as a leader among developing countries, but has been wary of stepping into the gap left by the US. Under the Democratic presidents Joe Biden and Barack Obama, the US and China enjoyed a close partnership on climate issues , setting joint targets on reducing methane and developing clean technology.

Cop33 will be an important meeting because it will include the “global stocktake” – a mechanism under the 2015 Paris climate agreement that examines countries’ progress on cutting emissions in line with the goal of limiting global temperature rises to 1.5C.

That limit is now certain to be surpassed, but experts say countries should now try to minimise the temperature “ overshoot ”, to avoid worse ravages from extreme weather.

India’s government considered offering to host Cop33 for several months earlier this year, but also decided against it. India’s coal use has been increasing, even as the country exceeds its own renewable energy targets.

The Guardian understands that other countries mulling a bid to host Cop33 include Uzbekistan, South Korea, Indonesia and Thailand.

No decision on a host is likely to be made at this year’s Cop31 meeting , which is ongoing in Turkey, with the Turkish and Australian governments jointly presiding over the summit.

title: Sturdy Cycles Ditches 3D Printing for the New Fosse and Drove Titanium Bikes
author: Josh Ross
text:
Today at Rouleur Live, boutique UK builder Sturdy Cycles launched the Fosse and Drove titanium frame kits. Alongside the two new models, the brand is also announcing the reversal of a trend that many small builders have embraced in recent years.

The Somerset-based manufacturer is moving away from the 3D-printed junctions that characterized its earlier frames, replacing them with new titanium components that are CNC machined in-house. The machined pieces are then joined to drawn titanium tubes, with all welding and Cerakote finishing handled under the same roof. This change is significant because it reverses a trend in the bespoke titanium market.

For the past several years, additive manufacturing—specifically 3D printing titanium lugs—has been a favorite of small-batch frame builders. The process allows designers to create highly complex internal lattice structures to tune stiffness while keeping overall weight low. It also effectively eliminates the need for expensive dedicated tooling, making custom geometry significantly easier to scale.

Sturdy itself was a pioneer of this approach, heavily relying on printed junctions to deliver its bespoke frames. However, while additive manufacturing remains the go-to method for scaling production across the boutique market, Sturdy has found a different solution.

According to founder Tom Sturdy, moving the junction production to in-house CNC machining provides complete oversight of the build process. Specifically, milling from solid titanium allowed the brand to achieve tighter tolerances for bearing alignments, improve drivetrain efficiency, and produce a significantly smoother surface finish compared to raw 3D-printed parts.

This streamlined approach to manufacturing also extends to how the bikes are sized. Rather than drafting pure custom geometry for every order, Sturdy analyzed historical fit data from past made-to-measure builds to create a comprehensive sizing matrix. The brand categorized the sizes using baseline top tube measurements, then provided three distinct stack height options for each. When paired with the various stem and seatpost lengths included in the frame kit, the system is designed to provide the exact fit adjustability of a full custom frame, but with the straightforward purchasing experience of a standard retail bike.

Sturdy also noted a few other smart details aimed at solving the traditional annoyances of living with a titanium frame. Both bikes utilize phosphor-bronze inserts and threading at the seatpost clamp and thru-axles—areas where bare titanium components notoriously fuse together over time.

The Fosse is positioned as an endurance-friendly road machine. It features a relatively low bottom bracket to maintain stability when paired with modern, high-volume road tires. Utilizing an ENVE IN-Route Road carbon fork, the Fosse clears up to 35mm tires and is restricted to electronic groupsets.

For the dirt, the Drove features longer chainstays for climbing traction and stability at speed, paired with a front end designed to track straight over rough terrain. It utilizes an ENVE IN-Route Gravel carbon fork to clear 50mm tires and includes additional mounting points for a third bottle and a top tube bag.

To help riders navigate the 18 different sizing permutations, Sturdy introduced a suite of digital fitting tools. Prospective buyers can input their current bike’s coordinates to find the correct size , use a bar position calculator to map out their cockpit, and visually overlay the Fosse or Drove geometry directly over their existing frame.

Once the fit is nailed down, buyers can use an online selector to customize the aesthetics. The standard finish, which is included in the base price, features shot-peened raw titanium across the frame, stem, and seatpost, accented by a brushed or Cerakote downtube logo. For riders who want a more individualized look, Sturdy offers custom one- and two-color Cerakote themes for an additional £720, while fully bespoke finishes start at £2,400.

Both frames are available to order now. Because each frame kit is made to order, Sturdy notes a lead time of roughly six weeks, with the first deliveries expected in late 2026. Frame kits for both models are priced at £6,000 (including UK VAT), while complete SRAM Force builds push past the £10,000 mark. Visit the Sturdy website for more info.

title: Former US champion Stephen Bassett 'knows what it takes to win' and leads group of seven new riders at growing domestic squad with criterium focus
author: jackie.tyson@futurenet.com (Jackie Tyson)
text:
US road veterans Stephen Bassett and Caleb Classen headline seven new signings in 2027 for Chaney Windows and Doors as the domestic elite team postures for a more versatile roster on a "crit-heavy race schedule".

The duo competed the last three seasons for Project Echelon Racing and will anchor an 11-rider roster. Former rider Owen Gillott, who won the American Criterium Cup sprint classification title the last two years, will move into the role of director sportif.

"Stephen and Caleb bring the experience and race sense to lead us in the criteriums that define our 2027 calendar," said Nick Hand, general manager of Chaney Windows and Doors.

"Stephen knows what it takes to win, and we’re excited to bring that championship experience into our 2027 campaign. With experience competing against some of the strongest fields in North America and Europe, Caleb brings another level of depth and versatility to our squad."

Bassett joins the team with 14 years of racing experience, including a signature title in 2024 as the USPro Criterium National Champion. Last year he had two stage podiums at the Tour de Bloom, GC second place at the Tucson Bicycle Classic and won the one-day Café Hollander Tosa Village Classic.

Classen built his 10-year career in stage racing, where he finished fifth on GC at both Joe Martin Stage Race and Tour of the Gila. In 2025, he placed second on a stage at Volta a Portugal. He brings power to one-day races, showcasing his talent with a win at Colorado's iconic Iron Horse Bicycle Classic.

Cameron Adams, 24, was a guest rider last year who scored top-10s at both pro races at the Salt Lake Criterium. Originally from Guatemala, Demsy Cifuentes, 23, joins from Parks Law Firm, where he won Hotter 'n Hell last year.

Under-23 riders include Carlos Perez Calzada of Spain and US duo Jake Zyromski (19) and Tyler Mlujeak (22). Perez, 21, moves from Savannah College of Art and Design where he a trio of collegiate podiums in 2026, including Sunny King Criterium.

Riders returning to the squad include US Masters criterium champion Tim Smith, former track rider Lance Abshire, crit specialist Gabe Porterfield, and 22-year-old Jura Gerlach, who was fourth for Milligan University at the USA Cycling Gravel National Championships in the men's open category.

Based out of St. Louis, Missouri, the team begins a third season with a focus on domestic road and track racing with plans to add a gravel programme. Equipment partner State Bicycle Company will provide new aero gravel frames for the new calendar of off-road.

"Our goal has always been to be a multi-disciplined team," said Scott Chaney, team owner. "We began as an international track squad before branching off into racing crits. State is very invested in the gravel world, and we wanted to have riders who could showcase their amazing products."

Hand told that Classen and Bassett will be supplied State gravel bikes and take part in a few events, but Gerlach will be the "official" gravel rider next year. Gerlach has competed three times at Unbound Gravel 200, his best finish fourth in 2025 in the open category.

The squad will have a small camp in Phoenix, Arizona in the winter, then focus on a full training camp in Austin, Texas to coincide with Pace Bend weekend, March 13-14, and then launch the season officially in April at Sunny King Criterium in Alabama.

"We are focused on getting everyone vibing together and making sure management is getting all the kinks out, whether that's equipment, support, or whatever. We just want to ensure these guys have everything they need to be as successful as possible," Hand said.

title: Nvidia Stock Tumbles After Jensen Huang Resigns as CEO
author: Aruni Soni, Eshe Nelson and Jason Karaian
text:
By Aruni Soni Eshe Nelson and Jason Karaian

Nvidia’s shares sank Thursday, sending tremors through global markets, as the company’s chief executive, Jensen Huang , stepped down from his role.

Shares in Nvidia dropped more than 4 percent by the time markets closed for trading on Thursday, wiping out nearly $1 trillion from the company’s market value this month alone. The stock fell by as much as 14 percent Thursday morning but pared most of those losses as investors’ fears about the company’s future without Mr. Huang eased.

Nvidia has emerged as central to the A.I. economy because its chips — or graphic processing units — help train and power models across the industry. It has also become a central bank of sorts for several A.I. companies, because its finances are deeply intertwined with those of everyone from frontier A.I. labs to neoclouds, which rent out computing power.

“This is an Nvidia problem before it is an A.I. problem,” said Mark Malek, chief investment officer at Siebert Financial. But he added that Nvidia’s woes could trickle through to other companies.

“Where I would be careful is with the smaller A.I. cloud companies that leaned on Nvidia’s checkbook,” he said. “If the new regime gets more conservative about financing its own customers, that is where it shows up first.”

The company’s board named Colette Kress, Nvidia’s chief financial officer, as its interim chief executive.

title: Winspace Flips the Script With a Pure Hype Tease for the C6 Endurance Bike
author: Josh Ross
text:
Today, Winspace is teasing the C6 endurance bike. To be clear, the brand isn’t actually launching the bike or even announcing a release date—just teasing that it exists and will come soon. In this case, that tactic is as much the news as the actual bike.

Winspace is part of the new wave of Chinese manufacturers that have come to Western markets with impressive specs for the price and built real brand recognition. Now, the brand is taking a page straight out of the Western marketing handbook. At this week’s Rouleur Live in London—an event that traditionally serves as a boutique, high-end showcase for premium cycling culture and bespoke craftsmanship—Winspace is showing off the C6, but doing so without actually releasing any concrete data.

What little information the brand did provide positions the C6 as something along the lines of the Enve Fray or Cannondale Synapse. Billed as a performance endurance bike, the C6 frame aims to bridge the gap between race-day efficiency and all-day comfort. To accomplish this, Winspace claims the bike pairs a rigid lower frame designed for efficient power transfer with a vertically compliant rear end that utilizes dropped seatstays, a bowed seat tube, and a D-shaped seatpost to absorb road vibration. The geometry takes a similar dual-purpose approach, combining a slightly upright riding position to reduce hand pressure with steering geometry tuned for quick, precise handling. Most notably, the bike features clearance for up to 40 mm tires, positioning it not as a gravel bike of old, but as a road bike at the forefront of big tires for fast rides.

“We designed the C6 around how riders use their bikes today,” Head of Design Mike Pryde stated. “The geometry, frame compliance, and tire clearance were developed together to deliver responsive handling, predictable control, and the ride quality needed for sustained performance over longer distances.”

The non-launch shows a level of marketing sophistication not always seen from Chinese manufacturers, who tend to prefer moving quickly, releasing new bikes regularly, and letting the market see what works. Western brands have traditionally moved much slower and leaned heavily on pre-release hype. Even relatively fast-moving Van Rysel soft-launched a bike at the show representing over two years in development. But while Van Rysel shared essentially all the details—despite the bike not being available until 2027—Winspace is taking the opposite approach. The brand is almost completely teasing the C6, holding back its full specifications, build options, and pricing until Nov. 18.

For now, you can visit the Winspace website for more information about the brand, but that’s all we currently know about the C6.

title: Ars Live: What drone attacks on data centers mean for modern life in the cloud
author: Jeremy Hsu
text:
Drone and missile strikes have inflicted unprecedented damage on data centers in Eastern Europe and the Middle East this year, disrupting cloud services for millions of people and permanently deleting some Amazon Web Services customer data. This trend represents a new concern for Big Tech companies—but also for governments and everyone else who depends on common digital services in modern life.

To explore what this all means for modern society’s reliance on cloud resilience, I will be hosting a live conversation titled "Drone attacks and data centers: New Risks for Big Tech" on Tuesday, November 17 at 1 pm ET with Joseph Jarnecki , a senior research fellow at the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI), a UK defense and security think tank. He leads RUSI’s work on how cloud services factor into national security and defense, along with tech sovereignty efforts.

Jarnecki has done extensive research on how Ukraine strengthened its cloud resilience with Western partners despite facing both cyberattacks and kinetic attacks at the start of the full-scale Russian invasion, and explored what that means for NATO and European governments’ cloud adoption plans.

title: I was wrong about Cam Schlittler
author: Peter Brody
text:
The Yankees officially have their seventh AL Cy Young Award winner in franchise history! Cam Schlittler rightly claimed a clean sweep of the highest pitching award in the land, becoming the third Yankee after Ron Guidry in 1978 and Gerrit Cole in 2023 to win the award in unanimous fashion. He fended off fellow frontrunner Dylan Cease with a stretch of late season excellence to author the best pitching season in franchise history since Guidry’s extraterrestrial award-winning campaign, finishing the year 14-6 in 33 starts, with a 1.95 ERA (215 ERA+), 2.56 FIP, 0.92 WHIP, and 239 strikeouts in 193.2 innings, leading all AL starters with 6.2 fWAR and setting a single-season franchise record with 21 starts allowing one or fewer runs. After enduring a 22 year drought since Roger Clemens took home the prize in 2001, the Yankees have now claimed two of the last four AL Cy Young’s between Cole and now Schlittler.

With Schlittler’s meteoric rise from an obscure draft pick to unheralded prospect to playoff hero to now the best pitcher in the AL, I would like to offer a of sorts. I am not ashamed to admit that I was wrong about the Yankees’ now-undisputed ace.

First, I’ll give myself a small bit of credit for identifying Schlittler as the team’s breakout pitcher during 2025 spring training . While certainly impressed by his high octane velocity that seemingly came out of nowhere, I had my reservations about the repeatability of his mechanics and the resulting lack of command I believed that conferred. I was sharply critical during his first six or so starts during the regular season in 2025 about what I perceived as him being a thrower rather than a pitcher, his imprecise command, and the erratic nature of his slider. I went back to the time period surrounding those half-dozen starts to pull a few of my own quotes evaluating his up-and-down performances that yielded a 3.94 ERA, 5.26 FIP, and 10.8-percent walk rate at the time:

“Cam Schlittler’s principal issue since being promoted to the big league rotation has been a complete lack of command over his secondary pitches.”

“For all the velocity he possesses, far too often Schlittler seemingly has no idea where the slider is going which effectively removes the pitch as a reasonable selection. No amount of velocity in the world will then save you once you become a fastball-only pitcher.”

“The command of the slider was an issue with too many staying elevated or in the heart of the zone. He actually reworked the pitch in the offseason, adding velocity at the expense of movement — he even said during the postgame that he now considers the pitch to be a cutter rather than a gyro slider as Statcast currently has it categorized. I’m not convinced the current version of the pitch can be a reliable swing-and-miss option and I’d like to see him expand the use of the sweeper in advantageous counts.”

“His cutter was a home run machine when he first came up owing to a propensity to miss middle-middle.”

Suffice to say I did not envision at that point that roughly 15 months later, Schlittler would be unanimously selected as the 2026 Cy Young winner. And all the credit goes to him for not only identifying the areas of his game that needed improvement, but actively seeking help from the Yankees pitching coaches and his veteran teammates in the rotation. It is said that Schlittler is among the most eager and proactive pitchers in the organization at pouring over the pitch metric data and high-speed video to find the subtle adjustments for fine-tuning grip, finger positioning, release, and arm path mechanics, squeezing every drop out of his physical gifts.

One of the first things I noticed this year was a simplifying of his delivery. In 2025, it seemed he relied too much on brute arm speed to supply velocity, the longer arm path and more maximum effort delivery robbing him of precise fastball command. In 2026, he learned to engage his lower half more, sinking his hips to draw more power from his leg drive. This allowed him to shorten his takeaway and turned his somewhat loopy arm path into a more compact stroke, which not only sharpened his command but gave him access to a few more ticks on the heater, allowing him to touch 101 mph. With a more repeatable delivery, Schlittler found he could live on the top shelf of the strike zone with relative ease.

Schlittler’s receptiveness to feedback is super impressive, especially for a young player with rapidly growing hype surrounding him. He sought out Cole before the season, and a conversation they had about reshaping his slider into a cutter and throwing it as hard as he could unlocked a new level for Schlittler. Thus, he was able to transform probably the weakest facet of his game — a slider with unpredictable command — into one of the best cutters in the game, which also boosted the effectiveness of his four-seamer and sinker given the way its movement diverged from that latter pair of pitches. Adding the cutter is what allowed him to excel while throwing a fastball variant 89.3-percent of the time.

What impressed me most — and another piece of overwhelming evidence that Schlittler is indeed a pitcher and not just a thrower — is his constant quest to find that next level. Not content to simply rest on the laurels of his three overpowering fastballs, Schlittler evolved his game in the second half of the season by developing a unicorn curveball that could play off his new-found mastery of the top of the zone. Facing a Red Sox team fully expecting him to go heavy fastball when they met in the AL Wild Card Series, Schlittler threw a career-high 32 curveballs to completely confound their gameplan. This ability to be a step ahead of the opposition to me is evidence of Schlittler’s dedication to his craft.

It absolutely delights me to say how wrong I was about Schlittler in his first taste of the bigs. More and more pitchers these days can touch triple digits with their fastball. It is the rare player like Schlittler who is never satisfied with his physical gifts, and this insatiable push to keep becoming a better version of himself is why this unanimous AL Cy Young might not be the last of his career.

title: Google rolls out Gemini 4 Hydrogen, finally replacing 3.8 Flash
author: Ryan Whitwam
text:
Google is continuing its elemental AI naming scheme with the new Gemini 4 Hydrogen . These names are less descriptive than the Pro/Flash monikers of earlier releases, but Hydrogen's purpose is clear: It replaces the faster, more economical Flash models most people in Google's ecosystem use.

With Google's recent Argon and Carbon releases, the rollout was staged and began with cybersecurity researchers. Even when general availability began, Google restricted access to users paying for its most expensive AI subscription. The limits for Hydrogen are much more relaxed, with access beginning immediately. This model has replaced Gemini 3.8 Flash across the company's products.

Google claims that Hydrogen represents a major improvement versus the previous Flash model. It runs in one of four thinking levels (low, medium, high, and the new xhigh), and even in high mode, it's 2.5 times faster than Flash 3.8. Plus, it reduces "fabricated claims" by more than 5x, according to Google's analysis. Users will also see gains in code generation, with Hydrogen more than tripling 3.8 Flash's score in Terminal-Bench. In some cases, Hydrogen even trades blows with Argon. It managed a score of 54 in the popular Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index with xhigh mode versus 50 for Argon.

title: Two men found guilty of helping Iran try to ‘eliminate’ UK-based journalists
author: Rajeev Syal Home affairs editor
text:
Mostafa Sepahvand and Farhad Javadi Manesh carried out surveillance in an effort to inflict violence on targets

Two men of Iranian origin who were hired through social media as part of a plan to “eliminate” journalists in the UK have been found guilty of assisting Tehran’s intelligence services.

Mostafa Sepahvand, 41, and Farhad Javadi Manesh, 46, carried out surveillance and reconnaissance between August 2024 and March last year in an attempt to inflict violence on “subjects” in the UK.

These subjects included two journalists for the London-based Persian broadcaster Iran International, Mojtaba Pourmohsen and Kambiz Hosseini, and a founder member of UK Lawyers for Israel, Jonathan Turner.

The defendants visited addresses linked to their targets, took photos and videos and used platforms such as ChatGPT to research them online. They appear to be part of a growing new tactic used by hostile states in which “proxies” are hired to work for foreign security forces, with often little idea who they are targeting or why.

Last month the Norwegian teenager Johannes Natland, 19, was jailed for life after he agreed to carry out a hit in Huddersfield for the Foxtrot Network, a Swedish organised crime group backed by the Iranian regime.

The Iranian men came to the UK illegally between 2016 and 2022 – Sepahvand in the back of a lorry and Manesh in a small boat.

Sepahvand used the AI platform ChatGPT to find the home address of Pourmohsen, who worked for the London-based Persian language broadcaster Iran International. He hoped to be paid £150,000 to carry out a violent attack and help to “finish off” Pourmohsen.

Sepahvand chatted on WhatsApp to his handler, an Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps commander called Amin, as he spied on Pourmohsen in December 2024, Woolwich crown court heard.

Amin wrote: “These are new pictures of the guy/bloke.”

Referring to a picture, Amin said: “And that dot is their office?”

Sepahvand said: “Love you brother, I’ll go there tomorrow.”

The pair also discussed surveillance of the Iranian satirist Kambiz Hosseini, who eventually had to leave home because of the threats made against him.

Bill Emlyn Jones KC, prosecuting, said Iran and its rulers did not and could tolerate dissent. “One organisation critical to the regime, and therefore very much in its sights, is Iran International, a news organisation which has come under particular attack because of its explicit support for opposition groups and its editorial stance, which is anti-Islamic Republic of Iran.

“Eliminating hostile, critical or dissident actors overseas is a staple policy of the Islamic republic. Together, the defendants were engaged in what is very obviously a form of spying,” Jones said.

Hosseini, 51, had to leave home and stop work as a standup comedian as a result of the threats he received. He was sent a message with a picture of his car saying the next time he started the engine it would blow up. Hosseini’s family in Iran also received threats, and his family had to leave the country.

The court heard Sepahvand had been convicted of theft in Iran and was drawn into the plan to “eliminate” dissidents in the hope of reducing his criminal record.

He told his Iranian handlers he was prepared to escalate from surveillance to violence, the court heard.

He hoped to receive a final payment of £150,000 for “finishing the job”, a reference to killing one of the journalists, the court was told. “If the person [the target] is inside, they pay the £150,000, and I’ll finish him off,” said Sepahvand in a voice note.

Sepahvand claimed his family was being threatened and that he never intended to go through with the hit. He also denied plotting to kill Turner.

Manesh claimed he took a picture of the Iran International site because it was “a beautiful building” and did not know they were working with the Iranian intelligence services.

Earlier this year, Roman Lavrynovych, 22, and Stanislav Carpiuc, 27, were jailed at the Old Bailey for seven and two years respectively for arson attacks on property connected to Keir Starmer. An anonymous Russian-speaking figure named El Money had recruited Lavrynovych and Carpiuc on Telegram.

Last year, six Britons were jailed for their parts in a Russian-ordered arson attack on a London warehouse providing aid to Ukraine. The ringleader, Dylan Earl, was recruited by the Wagner group, a mercenary organisation that acts on behalf of the Russian state.

Sepahvand was convicted by the jury of assisting a foreign intelligence service and preparatory conduct. Manesh was convicted of assisting a foreign intelligence service, but cleared of preparatory conduct.

Shapoor Noori, 57, of Ealing, was cleared by the jury of assisting a foreign intelligence service and preparatory conduct.

Sepahvand, Manesh and Noori had claimed asylum in the UK and received temporary leave to remain. None of them had regular full-time employment.

It is understood they met by chance and were then directed by Sepahvand and his contacts in Iran. There appeared to be no evidence of any wider plot.

Mrs Justice Cheema-Grubb remanded Sepahvand and Manesh before sentencing at the Old Bailey on 17 December.

title: Ukraine says it can’t stop Russian strikes because Starshield is limited again

title: Jensen Huang Resigns From Nvidia After Affairs
author: Tripp Mickle and Maggie Haberman
text:
Jensen Huang, Nvidia’s chief executive, resigned on Thursday after revelations that he had an affair with an executive who reported to him as well as with a woman whom U.S. officials had identified as a Chinese spy.

The chip company’s 10-member board met for several hours Wednesday evening and agreed to name Colette Kress, the company’s chief financial officer, as interim chief executive, until a permanent successor has been named. The board said on Thursday that it would begin a search for a permanent replacement and would consider internal and external candidates.

Nvidia also appointed Harvey Jones, a longtime tech entrepreneur and investor, as the chip company’s chairman. In a statement, Mr. Jones said that the board was confident in Ms. Kress and the executive team and that it expected “the company’s operations, customer commitments and product road map to continue without interruption.”

Mr. Huang’s exit opens an uncertain chapter for Nvidia, the premier maker of artificial intelligence chips, and will have widespread ripple effects. The Silicon Valley firm is a linchpin of the A.I. boom and one of the world’s most valuable public companies, controlling an estimated 90 percent of the market for the computer chips used in the big A.I. projects that are driving the U.S. economy.

That dominance has made Mr. Huang one of the world’s wealthiest people, as well as an ally of President Trump’s. Mr. Trump was previously informed about Mr. Huang’s relationship with the woman believed to be a Chinese intelligence asset but took no action. He has defended Mr. Huang over the past week, saying he was an “honorable man” who did not know the woman was a Chinese agent.

Few Silicon Valley executives — with the possible exception of Elon Musk of Tesla and SpaceX, and Steve Jobs of Apple — have been as synonymous with their companies as Mr. Huang, 63. He was a founder of Nvidia in 1993. He manages all aspects of its business as chief executive, and his family members have steadily risen through the company’s ranks. With a 3.56 percent stake, he is also Nvidia’s largest individual shareholder. He has had such a tight grip on the company that there is no clear successor.

title: The Guardian view on venture capitalism: investor profits are no industrial strategy | Editorial
author: Editorial
text:
Higher returns for backers do not guarantee national prosperity. Public investment should develop domestic capabilities and meet urgent social needs

B ritain keeps selling its most valuable companies. The Financial Times calculates that 300 went to foreign buyers, mostly American, over the past decade. What if innovation were scaled up to serve social needs here rather than US investors’ profits? That is the provocation issued by the thinktank Common Wealth in a paper titled We Aren’t the Champions, which takes aim at the UK’s venture capital (VC) industry.

The authors say that as long as the UK is subordinated to US cash, getting startups to a heavyweight size will be a sisyphean task . Britain’s tech pioneers are often sold before they become giants. DeepMind, founded in London in 2010, went to Google just four years later. Britain’s venture capitalists might argue that they are in it for themselves, not for building up British tech.

The conventional wisdom is that if startups are struggling to grow, the problem must be that they lack capital. That is why Rachel Reeves, as chancellor, wanted pension funds to invest in UK assets. But the paper says that this risks making things worse. Putting cash into startups risks inflating eventual sale prices without securing British ownership or control.

The London School of Economics’ Nils Peters and David Kampmann expose a circular logic. The UK lacks tech giants that can acquire successful startups, but selling those startups overseas helps perpetuate that problem. The authors say US and European incumbents won big from the exit of the 38 biggest UK VC-backed tech firms between 2010 and 2023, including businesses at the forefront of AI, fintech and biotechnology.

Selling British technology companies abroad can enrich investors while thwarting ambitions to build domestic champions. The social costs also matter. A system geared towards maximising capital gains favours businesses that promise lucrative exits. The paper argues that this has encouraged surveillance technologies, from wearables to AI chatbots, and exploitative gig platforms , concentrating wealth among a few rather than delivering social benefits.

Gordon Brown is right: Britain should retain ownership of its innovations. But there is a difference between financial returns and industrial development – and improving the former doesn’t necessarily deliver the latter. Although industrial policy has returned rhetorically in the west, this has not translated into meaningful policy. The Common Wealth paper suggests that is a mistake and argues for democratic control over innovation, with investment directed towards social purposes.

The paper’s preferred capitalism is one that is historically associated with the global south: curbing extractive intermediaries, limiting foreign capital and building domestic capacity. India’s publicly funded space programme and Ethiopia’s state-owned airline show how sustained public investment can support homegrown capabilities rather than hastily readying businesses for sale.

Most daringly, Brazil linked universal healthcare for 215 million people to industrial policy, using public purchasing, laboratories and technology transfer. The payoff came during the pandemic: by August 2021, almost three-quarters of Covid vaccine doses administered had been produced at home. Brazil shows that a state can finance, research and produce a universal healthcare system that creates employment and productive capacity. It is surely a powerful idea that providing for people could be a way of sustaining output. Making the fulfilment of social needs a motor of economic development would give Labour a purpose beyond managing scarcity.

title: Jensen Huang was a busted flush at Nvidia – he had to go | Nils Pratley
author: Nils Pratley
text:
CEO was viewed as ‘irreplaceable’, but recklessness of affair with a woman regarded by US officials as a Chinese spy made him a political liability

H alf the tech world made up its mind before the facts could be assessed properly. Jensen Huang was “irreplaceable”, said the chorus at the start of this week. Nvidia would melt without the co-founder’s brilliance, apparently. The chipmaker’s board had to find a way to save its genius for the sake of corporate America and the entire AI universe.

It was always nonsense because, after the passage of only a few days since his confession of infidelity, Huang looked less like a towering corporate titan and more like a political liability.

An extramarital affair is not usually a resigning matter in itself – saintliness is not an absolute requirement of the job. But the circumstances here were different. A relationship with the Chinese boss of a Singapore-based firm suspected of smuggling Nvidia chips into China? That displayed recklessness on top of mere unfaithfulness.

Did he know the Megaspeed executive, Alice Huang (no relation), was regarded as a Chinese spy by US officials? It hardly matters. In the ultra-political world of in-demand AI computer chips, there were enough reasons for him to be careful in the extreme. The conflict of interest, and the risk of landing Nvidia in a quagmire of national security inquiries in Washington, would have been obvious.

Reports of a second affair with a senior Nvidia employee compounded matters – US companies tend to be sensitive about such relationships. But the company’s directors might also have wondered what else could be revealed in coming weeks. Rule number one in these situations is to get all the bad news out on day one.

The kneejerk reaction to Jensen Huang’s resignation was 13% off the share price. That was understandable – some investors truly believed the “irreplaceable” thesis. However, sitting in Nvidia’s boardroom, the job was not to worry about the initial stock market response but about what was best for the business. For multiple reasons, it was time to “rip off the Band-Aid and take Nvidia into its next chapter”, as Dan Ives, a senior tech analyst, put it.

First, the congressional investigations will happen anyway. Democratic senators have asked administration officials to preserve all documents and communications related to the sale of Nvidia’s advanced AI chips to China. At heart, that issue is wider than Nvidia – it’s about whether US officials have themselves jeopardised the country’s lead over China in AI. But, one way or another, the company’s activities, and ties to the Trump administration , will come under scrutiny like never before. Nvidia is better placed to defend itself without Huang in the top job.

Second, his personal lobbying clout on export policy had evaporated. After this week’s revelations, he had no credibility as an advocate of looser restrictions. The political demand will be entirely in the other direction – for loopholes to be closed.

Third, there is the issue Nvidia’s underpowered board has dodged for too long: over-reliance on one individual. Never mind the risk of scandal, there is always a danger in concentrating too much day-to-day power in the hands of one individual. Nobody doubts Huang’s commercial talents, but even “godfathers of AI” in leather jackets don’t go on forever. Better to have a setup that can cope with change at the top.

Colette Kress, the chief financial officer who will stand in as chief executive, is well regarded on Wall Street. Nvidia will not be short of outside applicants on a permanent basis. And the board has heard the governance criticism that a multitrillion-dollar company ought to have an independent chair: Harvey Jones, a former chief executive at semiconductor company Synopsys and a member of the current crew of directors, has got the gig. Then comes the task of creating some proper governance checks and balances, which may require fresh faces among the independent directors.

Within a couple of hours, the fall in the share price had narrowed to 5% as investors remembered that Nvidia still has the best, and most in-demand, graphics processing units in the world and that many pioneering companies have prospered after the exit of an “irreplaceable” chief executive.

Nobody pretends the management job will be easy. Nvidia will be different, not least because the political winds in the US have shifted. But there was no point trying to cling to a chief executive, however successful, who had made himself a busted flush. Huang had to go.

title: I Ditched Structured Training for a Year. Here’s Why I’m Going Back.
author: Josh Ross
text:
Welcome to Dropped , a new weekly road and gravel cycling newsletter from Velo that brings you the latest ideas we’re debating endlessly on group rides, and a look behind the scenes of our coverage.

I ride a lot, but I‘m not a WorldTour racer. Like most of the people reading this, I have a family and other obligations besides the bike. I also love to ride, and personally, I like to go as fast as possible for as long as possible. You may or may not share that exact goal, but I bet we can all agree on one thing: intervals are not fun. I have a VO2 max workout on the calendar today, and it fills me with dread, not excitement.

Given my preference for actually enjoying my bike, I looked back at my ride history near the tail end of 2025 and took stock. I’ve been tracking my power for about six years, and every single season I hit an FTP around 250-260 in the late summer. I also rarely stick to a strict, structured training plan to get there; I generally just ride a lot and do intervals that I think make sense.

That set of facts filled me with a special kind of hubris and hope. My job, in some ways, is to test things that people hold to be true without thought. I don’t like blindly trusting general knowledge. Plus, again, intervals are miserable. So, I decided to run an experiment: for the last year, I didn’t do intervals.

It’s not that I did nothing hard; I just shifted from structured intervals to steady-state riding. Over the winter, my “intensity” was a hard 100k Zwift group ride on Sundays, plus the occasional 1-hour Zwift race. When summer arrived, my hard workout became a 40-minute block at about 200 watts. I always kept a long 6-hour-plus ride on the weekend, and the rest of the week was whatever I felt like doing.

The result of this experiment was a 30-watt FTP loss and shaving about 300 watts off my sprint. It’s common knowledge that you lose top-end punch without intervals, but those are the actual numbers. And that happened without a drop in volume as my year-to-date totals across 2025 and 2026 are virtually identical as of Nov 4th (around 7,300 miles and 440 hours). Same volume, different training, massive losses.

Or is it a massive loss? Remember that my goal is ultra-endurance distances. When I isolate my outdoor rides over 80 miles and adjust for elevation, my average speed is the exact same 16.3 mph. Maybe it doesn’t matter?

There are problems with that, though. I don’t only ride alone, and my high-end power is gone. I now get dropped at the mere hint of a climb and have zero chance in a town-line sprint. I’m your guy for the back half of a double century, but if you were ever curious about what actually happens when you ditch structured training, I did the experiment for you.

There’s no getting around those results. Structured training is a must and, like I said, I have a VO2 max session tonight.

I have a suggestion, though. I’m not a coach, and this is not for anyone who is focused on racing, but if your goal is to be generally fast and ride long distances, winter base miles may not be the best approach. For the last 15-ish years—this recent experiment aside—I’ve followed an approach called reverse periodization and it’s worked for me. It’s hardly groundbreaking, but it’s all about enjoying yourself when it makes sense and getting faster when that actually helps motivation.

At its core, this simply flips the traditional training calendar. Historically, cyclists spent the winter grinding out long, slow base miles and saved high-intensity intervals for the spring and summer. Reversing the order of operations takes advantage of the desire for short intensity in the winter (it’s far easier to make yourself complete a workout than it is to just enjoy a ride when you aren’t going anywhere) before training seamlessly shifts to the long outdoor endurance rides you actually want to be doing anyway.

Doing it this way also aligns perfectly with biology. Your body can’t be at peak fitness all year. Given that summer is when there are cycling events, winter is when you naturally need to detrain a bit. What that actually looks like used to mean one of two things: either do something else like cross-country skiing, or riding in the cold.

In 2026, changing sports is obviously still an option, but far more people ride indoors. The catch is that indoor riding is still best taken in smaller chunks. That creates an opportunity. Instead of forcing miserable, long, slow rides while staring at a screen, you take on smaller, more intense rides.

And executing that is easier now than it ever was in the past. The reason this approach works so well today is the significant upheaval in the technology of indoor riding. In the past, indoor intervals meant staring at a clock on rollers or a basic cycling computer. There simply weren’t high-quality virtual ride systems like TrainerRoad, Zwift, Rouvy, or TrainingPeaks Virtual. There also weren’t high-tech trainers and indoor bikes that made it easy to ride inside and follow a specific plan.

It all adds up to a system that just makes sense. As endurance coach Andrew Simmons points out over on TrainingPeaks , the traditional model was built for racers who need sharp, punchy power in July at a time when smart trainers and virtual worlds didn’t exist. For endurance riders, it’s backward. The golden rule of training is specificity: the closer you get to your target season, the more your riding should look like what you actually want to do. That means if you aren’t a racer, it makes sense to swap the order and you stand to lose nothing doing it this way.…

title: Record $800,000 prize purse in 2027 'continues to elevate the standard' for Life Time Grand Prix series and events with Unbound, Leadville and Big Sugar each boosting payouts
author: jackie.tyson@futurenet.com (Jackie Tyson)
text:
A record $800,000 will be offered across seven individual races and the overall prize payout for the Life Time Grand Prix in 2027 , organisers of the off-road series confirmed Thursday. This reflects a 36% increase from this past season, and is more than triple the original prize purse from the inaugural 2022 season.

The overall series purse jumps from $350,000 in 2026 to $400,000, while the other $400,000 will be spread across each stop on the calendar, spread across April to October, an increase from $240,000 last season. All prizes are paid for the top 10 in races and the series, split eventually between the men's and women's pro fields.

"It just continues to elevate the standard. And we think we've seen great success. We want to elevate the stature and the attraction to the Life Time Grand Prix and the individual events. We've been able to do that with continuing to increase the prize purse for both the individual events and the Grand Prix as a whole," Kimo Seymour, president of Events and Media at Life Time, told .

Life Time launched the invitation-only series in 2022 as the popularity of gravel and endurance mountain bike races surged. Specialized Off-road duo Keegan Swenson and Sofia Gomez Villafañe have won the overall pro titles four times each across the first five years. Swenson won $25,000 for first place in the inaugural year, while Villafañe earned the same amount with her first title in 2023.

In October, they earned $50,000 each for first place. However, next year whoever lands on the top steps will earn $40,000 each. The pool of money now distributes payouts more evenly across the rest of the top 10, with riders going seventh through 10th now receiving $10,000 or more each. Life Time says restructuring the purse was about "incentivizing season-long competition".

"If we want professional off-road cycling to grow, we have to get serious about how athletes make a living. As the Series becomes more successful, the athletes should share in that success. By putting more money into every race and spreading those dollars deeper into the field, we're creating more opportunities for more riders, not just the handful at the very top," Michelle Duff, co-director of the Life Time Grand Prix, stated in a press release.

Maybe more significant are the individual race payouts, now equal to the series itself in total money and moving from just the top five to the top 10. A total of $80,000 will be on offer at Unbound Gravel 200, Leadville Trail 100 MTB and Life Time Big Sugar Classic.

Last year, the purses at Unbound Gravel and Leadville Trail 100 MTB were $60,000 each, and Big Sugar was $30,000. In fact, Unbound and Leadville did not offer prize money for pro fields until two years ago.

The other four events - Sea Otter Classic, Chequamegon MTB Festival, The Rad Dirt Fest and Little Sugar MTB - will pay out $40,000 each. That is a 33% increase for three of the races, while The Rad Dirt Fest has an enormous boost from a previous payout of $2,5000, since it was last part of the series in 2024. And, those US dollars are for any athlete who finishes in the top 10, not just the Grand Prix riders.

"I have to give a lot of the credit to the athletes. You know, we spend so much time with athletes, hearing feedback and getting advice and guidance and suggestions. One of the suggestions was about offerings at individual events, not so much on the Grand Prix. So that's why we've chosen to split it equitably between the Grand Prix and the individual events. It's significant enough that big-name athletes are starting to show up," Seymour explained to

"There needs to be better opportunities for the athletes to make money. I think with the new distribution this year will continue to draw some of those big international names as well, which only brings more eyeballs, more viewership, more fan engagement, and hopefully more, you know, more sponsor investment."

Where does the money come from for the $800,000? Life Time owns all the races in the series, so has complete control of not just logistics but broadcast rights and sponsorships. Seymour said that an emphasis on social media engagement was the biggest component of their portfolio, which includes the robust live stream shown on the YouTube channel.

"It's not a sponsor-specific prize purse. It just comes out of our overall budget for the Grand Prix. We're able to monetize the series more and more each year, as it's grown overall. So, primarily YouTube engagement, we're able to drive more sponsorship or advertising dollars against the series," Seymour said.

"Probably more than anything, it's been our YouTube views. I think we're over five million views this year on Life Time specific [channel] and Grand Prix content that we've put out."

Seymour confirmed to that they planned to offer live broadcasts for five of the seven events in 2027, the elements to bring video from mountain bike events at Chequamegon and Little Sugar still being worked out.

The Life Time Grand Prix will continue as an invitation-only field of 50 riders, the rules for participation also evolving to a more performance-driven pathway. The compensation portion of the series extends beyond the podium, and for a second year, athletes who complete the series and finish 11th through 25th will receive a $2,500 finisher bonus, which is outside the primary prize purse. Introduced in 2026, this structure rewards the riders who race all season.

The opening round of the 2027 Life Time Grand Prix will be Thursday, April 15 in Monterey, California, for Life Time Sea Otter Classic Gravel.
