title: Zimbabwean author Simbarashe Kundizeza cleared of using AI to write prize-winning story
author: Rachel Savage in Johannesburg and agencies
text:
After a month-long investigation it was concluded that Kundizeza’s story The Blue Fighter, which won the £10,000 Caine prize, was ‘human-written’

The Zimbabwean author Simbarashe Kundizeza has been cleared of using AI to write a prize-winning short story, after the prestigious Caine prize for African writers concluded that his entry was “human-written” after a month-long investigation.

Kundizeza’s story The Blue Fighter , which charts the declining fortunes of a family after the father invests in fish tanks, was announced as the winner of the £10,000 prize on 6 October.

Five days later, the Atlantic published an article titled “Yet another literary prize winner seems to be AI”, in which the author and journalist Vauhini Vara said the AI-detection software Pangram, which itself uses AI, had deemed the story to be almost completely artificially generated.

The Caine prize chair, Ellah Wakatama, said in a statement : “From our detailed investigation, we feel the evidence is clear: The Blue Fighter was human-written. We now look forward to awarding and celebrating Simbarashe Steyn Kundizeza … before the end of the year.”

She said: “When concerns were raised, we have a duty as an organisation to look at them carefully and fairly,” adding that the prize had taken a “human-centred” approach to its investigation.

“Our review included interviews with the author, the 2026 judging panel and The Shallow Tales Review, where the story was first published,” Wakatama said. “It also included independent and expert-led metadata analysis of drafts written by the author.”

Kundizeza, who had strongly denied using generative AI to write the story, said he was “relieved” that the allegations had been dismissed after the investigation. “It was not necessary in the first place, I am happy to put all this behind me and continue with my writing journey,” he said.

Vara’s article prompted outrage online, with many claiming that Black writers, and Africans in particular, were being unfairly singled out by allegations of the use of AI.

Associated Press contributed to this report

title: AI helped UK defy expectations – but will economy’s resilience fizzle out?
author: Richard Partington Senior economics correspondent
text:
Despite John Healey’s defiance, the economy faces threats from a tech slowdown and energy bills this winter

AI helps UK economy grow at fastest pace for more than two years

The forecasters were clear when John Healey became chancellor in July: Britain’s resilience to the war in the Middle East would not last. The global economic headwinds were too strong, inflation was beginning to rise and growth would slow to a trickle.

Four months into the job, the economy is continuing to defy expectations after growing by 0.7% in the third quarter – the fastest expansion in two and a half years. It puts the UK on course to be the second-fastest growing G7 economy this year.

On his first day in Downing Street the memo from the Treasury showed the most optimistic City analyst expected 0.3% quarterly growth. Most had pencilled in a figure close to zero. Some were warning that the UK could edge towards a recession.

Despite the gloomy outlook households have continued to spend and business investment has powered ahead, driven by the rollout of AI.

Underneath the bonnet, growth is being spearheaded by IT and professional services – together contributing about half of the rise in activity. As the central sectors in the AI boom, that is hardly surprising – with analysts at ING suggesting the strength in IT was “very clearly a datacentre story” thanks to the UK’s status as a leading destination in Europe for investment.

Overall, Deutsche Bank estimates that AI-related spending has added about 0.3% to 0.4% to GDP growth this year. It is clear to see why Healey is keen to build on the groundwork laid by his immediate predecessor, Rachel Reeves, to harness AI amid government efforts to court global business investment.

Meanwhile, household consumption is up by 1.6% so far this year – helped by spending over the warm summer months even as consumers faced a living standards squeeze because the Iran war fuelled a surge in petrol and diesel prices.

However, the fear is that the UK’s initial resilience to the global economic storm emanating from the Middle East will soon fizzle out.

Both of Britain’s recent growth engines face a tougher period ahead.

After the US midterm elections and revelations at the chipmaker Nvidia , the outlook for the AI investment boom is less certain. Financial markets have been rocked in recent weeks amid fears that a bubble in AI stocks could be about to burst . A slowdown in technology investment could hit the UK. Still, the hope is that swelling demand for AI will not evaporate overnight.

For households, however, a tough winter lies ahead. Energy bills are poised to increase by about a quarter in January, with the average annual household gas and electricity bill expected to climb to more than £2,000. Analysts say it is hard to see how consumer spending would not come under greater pressure in the new year.

In the latest data there were some early warning signs: retail sales and consumer discretionary spending fell in September. Real wage growth is cooling and the headline inflation rate is on track to reach a fresh peak of close to 5% next year.

With growth proving resilient, the Bank of England will feel emboldened to raise interest rates to combat imported inflation. City investors expect at least two more quarter-point increases to 4.5% before the end of next year. That will hit the brakes on the economy and add to the cost of living squeeze.

At last month’s budget Healey struck a defiant tone by arguing that the UK could continue to defy forecasters expectations. That task, however, is becoming increasingly tough.

title: Our verdict on Lawson earning a 2027 F1 extension
author: Jon Noble
text:
Liam Lawson and Arvid Lindblad will continue to race for Racing Bulls in 2027, with Red Bull electing against what would have been a huge Formula 1 driver sacking.

Here's what our team makes of the move to keep Lawson and Lindblad and not promote Formula 2 title contender Nikola Tsolov into a race seat.

An existential question has been answered

Very few driver decisions have felt as right as Lawson getting a fresh contract with Racing Bulls.

He has been superb this year. Yes, there are still some rough edges to smooth out, but he has been fast throughout, consistently strong, delivering technical input that his engineers have loved, and brilliantly able to shut out all the noise regarding the doubts over his future.

But there is a wider significance to Lawson getting a stay, and it's one I mentioned in Monday's From the Paddock newsletter . The Lawson decision was almost existential for Racing Bulls in telling us what that team is really about.

Sign up to our newsletter to be in with a chance of winning a signed Valtteri Bottas Cadillac F1 cap.

Is it an outfit that, under Alan Permane, can stand on its own two feet, take its own decisions and plot a path that is only focused on making itself better?

Or is it simply a puppet for sister squad Red Bull, a testing ground and training school for its future drivers, even if that means some short-term pain in rushing rookies through?

After the season Lawson has had, it would have made no sense for Racing Bulls to drop him and throw away all the good momentum it has built up. So keeping him for now gives us the answer about what Racing Bulls is about.

Tsolov has a bright future in F1, but time is on his side to make that step up.

The best decision for all involved

Pretty sure this is the best decision for Racing Bulls and in the future for Red Bull.

Both Lawson and Lindblad - a rookie, let's not forget - have shown that they can bring home the results when everything goes as planned over a race weekend.

Both are capable of being a replacement for Isack Hadjar or Max Verstappen if either of them slip on a banana skin. Red Bull knows what Lawson can bring to them if required, so he is a good measure of what Lindblad could potentially bring too.

Having Tsolov in the background and doing a few FP1 sessions will prepare him for an introduction in 2028.

As far as I'm concerned, it's the correct decision for all involved.

Credibility for Racing Bulls

If Racing Bulls is to be at all seen as an F1 team in its own right, with its own ambitions and dreams and what have you, rather than a pure Red Bull talent farm, then yeah, Lawson pretty much had to be kept on. Tsolov may end up faster down the line. For all we know, he may be faster already. But the kind of efficient scoring that Lawson has provided this year a rookie cannot match - I would say that's a rule in F1.

So Tsolov-for-Lawson would be nakedly sacrificing Racing Bulls's present for the senior Red Bull team's future, and every decision like that makes it less and less palatable for Red Bull to own two teams in F1. Only if Racing Bulls has its own aspirations can it be allowed to continue, and a new deal for Lawson buys some credibility in my eyes.

Marko would have dropped Lawson long ago

At the height of his powers, Helmut Marko would have ditched Lawson ages ago.

Lawson had his shot at the top team, didn't make it, and will likely not be given that chance again.

Now Marko's no longer in charge, and this is the biggest indicator yet that Racing Bulls is not Toro Rosso; developing young drivers is no longer the only, or primary, end goal for this team.

You can't blame Red Bull. Instead of a team that cost and lost money to run like Toro Rosso, Racing Bulls is now a multi-billion dollar entity. Constructors' championship finishing position is not the only definition of value in an F1 business anymore.

Taking risks with a team built with the acceptance of losing money is one thing. Taking risks with a team worth billions is another.

None of this is to criticise the decision it has made, as Lawson is a worthy F1 driver. It's just to point out yet more evidence that Racing Bulls is acting and being run like its own team.

Lawson would be wise to find an exit route

Lawson is in a fantastic position now and has been one of the star drivers of the season, but he should already be thinking about exit routes for 2028.

Tsolov is going to be waiting in the wings next year, and there's no reason why Racing Bulls might be faced with the exact same 'three into two' dilemma for 2028.

This time Lawson was the overwhelmingly logical pick, next time he might not be and, given Red Bull leaves those decisions until late in the season, he doesn't want to suddenly be left without a seat for 2028.

So he'd be wise to try to follow the Pierre Gasly and Carlos Sainz playbook of finding another driver Red Bull decides it's done with you.

Adds to an excellent redemption arc

I've got a lot of time for this career redemption arc. Lawson at the Red Bull senior team always felt like an uncomfortable fit to me, right from when it was announced. I certainly hadn't seen anything to suggest he would solve the team's second-driver problem.

Red Bull's bungling of what followed didn't help, but that ill-fated, two-race spell could've marked the beginning of the end of Lawson's F1 career.

Instead, what's followed has revealed plenty about his mental resolve - because he's had to process a lot these past 20 months yet has been absolutely unflappable.

Driving for the top teams is what every driver craves, but it doesn't have to be the be-all and end-all and, if you don't make it, it doesn't automatically consign you to career collapse.

Lawson's proved emphatically this year that he deserves a place in F1. This contract extension was therefore the only acceptable outcome.

title: Cavaliers 115, Knicks 107: “Credit them, but…”
author: Moritz Wollert
text:
As sports fans, our teams give us plenty to think about and then some. They give us stuff to bicker, to complain, to ramble about. We follow their every move meticulously, we break down the potential of prospective grocery baggers and hail them as the next coming. We love to read or listen to others doing the same, even or especially if we do not agree with their viewpoints. Lucky fanatics get something to cheer about every once in a while – consider that box checked by our beloved New York Knickerbockers lately.

Understandably, that focus on one team, that love for one franchise can lead to kind of a narrow view on things at times. Nothing wrong with that; fandom doesn’t have to be rational, it doesn’t have to explain itself. And it does not necessarily have to involve the other team’s perspective or, frankly, the other team at all. At times though, that group in the different colored jerseys is the biggest answer to the question you have regarding your own squad’s performance.

Last night felt exactly like that kind of game where the Knicks did a lot of stuff well, but in the end the Cleveland Cavaliers just did most of it a little bit better. And when the Knicks didn’t do something as well, it was also the Cavaliers who had a hand in that. From the opening tip, it was obvious that the Cavs wanted this one – analytically and this time around actually in reality, too. They remembered last Saturday when New York rained on their Rocket Arena parade on the second night of a back-to-back; they surely remembered the last time they visited Madison Square Garden. And it looked like they were tired of the narrative that had them as the soft wannabes that can’t keep up when the orange and blue drivers push the pedals to the metal.

Cavaliers put an end to Knicks’ winning streak

Donovan Mitchell lived in the lane for most of the night; every high slip screen was an automatic downhill and kick opportunity for the team from Ohio, and their old and new length bothered the smaller Knicks for long stretches of the game. Peyton Watson might not be able to hit the water from the Verrazzano Bridge right now, but he sure can impact a game defensively. A lot of the Ohioans were feeling good about themselves; Tyrese Proctor and Meleek Thomas gave youthful, quality energy off the bench. And then, of course, there was James Harden. That guy who is a poster child for a lot of ugly wrongs in the modern game, the one who has been awful all year long so far but decided to show up for this one and give his team a vintage performance in the very building he crapped the postseason bed in just half a year ago.

So even if, at least in Harden’s case, it’s hard to stomach, let’s follow Knicks Fan in Jerusalem’s proposal from the Postgame Thread that gave this text its headline. Let’s credit the Cavaliers for a game well played, for shots hit, for storms weathered. But as the headline and our friend in Israel suggested, there’s another side to the story, a “but”. Tipping our collective cap to the Cavs sure doesn’t mean the Knicks can’t do a lot of things better in the future. Jalen Brunson had a good scoring game yet failed to deliver any rhythm to the offense. Too many times the ball just stuck on the perimeter (a particular problem for OG Anunoby right now), and there wasn’t nearly enough off-ball movement to stretch a much bigger defense that wants you to finish over their size.

That size played quite a role in yesterday’s contest, be it on the boards or in the passing lanes. Unfortunately, the Knicks won’t get any taller, that’s for sure. Mike Brown tried to counter Cleveland’s length by going to Mohamed Diawara early in the absence of Jordan Clarkson. Mo had a nice drive and, in theory, could be a solution for physical matchup problems like this one, but clearly isn’t there yet. The young Frenchman seems unsure about himself, plays hesitantly, and is missing the wide-open shots he knocked down in his sleep last season. His defense mostly looks good but not good enough to warrant a bigger role yet.

So, what’s happening with Mikal Bridges?

Aside from plenty of mental lapses, missing open shots was a problem for Josh Hart last night as well, but we excuse the veteran as he clearly had to shake off some rust after his injury break. That doesn’t change the fact that his lack of consistent outside shooting can become an issue at times, especially against good teams that willingly put roaming defenders on him. Normally, he adds so many other intangibles that you can live with it in the bigger picture more often than not. In Mikal Bridges’ case, though, well, what’s there right now? Hounding defense? Don’t see it consistently. A presence off the ball? Nope. Secondary scoring? Corner threes? Emotion? Desperation? Anything?

Bridges once again played an uneventful, meager 17 minutes in this one. Plenty of the other guards – Deuce McBride, Landry Shamet, and Tyler Kolek – currently do everything Bridges is paid for and actually a bit more. The longer this situation drags on, the louder Mike Brown will hear the question: When will you make a change to the starting lineup? It’s easy to understand why he’s reluctant; he sure doesn’t want to create an internal problem by benching someone who did his part in winning a championship last year. But what if the problem is creating itself? There’s a tipping point to everything.

For the Knicks, this game won’t be one, and it shouldn’t be. There might be some stuff to think about, though, going forward. Just like we want to have it as fans.

title: Michael Carrick was just the latest fall guy for Manchester United’s dysfunctional hierarchy | Jamie Jackson
author: Jamie Jackson
text:
Disastrous decisions and confused appointments have been a constant theme at Old Trafford since Sir Alex Ferguson’s retirement in 2013

F or a window into the alarming dysfunction at Manchester United that Michael Carrick failed to manage and caused his sacking , consider the case of Eddie Howe, initially a favourite to succeed the 45-year-old before Mauricio Pochettino’s emergence as the chosen one.

The former Newcastle manager had been Jason Wilcox’s choice to take over from Carrick. Howe was also the favoured candidate of Dan Ashworth, Wilcox’s predecessor as United’s director of football, to follow Erik ten Hag after the Dutchman’s sacking in October 2024. Except Wilcox disagreed and Sir Jim Ratcliffe went with Wilcox’s man, Ruben Amorim, and that December Ashworth departed only five months after joining.

At that juncture Wilcox was the technical director. Now he is United’s highest-ranking football executive, the powerbroker. He was able, apparently with a straight face, to recommend to Ratcliffe that Howe, nearly two years after he rejected him, should become United’s eighth permanent No 1 in the 13 and a half years since Sir Alex Ferguson retired.

If following this is difficult, making sense of it is near impossible. Should London’s West End need a new farce then look no further than the wacky world of Ratcliffe and the football department he leads, which is also headed up by Omar Berrada, the chief executive, and is proving a disjointed, illogical operation.

Yet if this meant Carrick was dealt a treacherous hand, it is also true that he should have played it better. This, after all, is the job of a football coach: to somehow make wine from water – even if the water is murky, and may need purifying first.

José Mourinho, one of Carrick’s predecessors, from May 2016 to December 2018, showed how – to a degree. Mourinho stated famously that leading United to second place in 2017-18 (with 81 points, 19 behind Manchester City) was one of his finest achievements. This from a serial winner who broke the United-Arsenal duopoly of the Premier League to take Chelsea to consecutive crowns (2004-05 and 2005-06), and made history in Italy by guiding Inter to the treble in 2009-10.

Mourinho’s billing of that second place was down to having to negotiate a similar shambles, overseen by Ed Woodward, the then executive vice-chair.

The Portuguese’s opening campaign ended with the Carabao Cup and Europa League collected despite, like Carrick, having to deal with a hierarchy convinced that it knew better than the man it hired as the football expert.

Here we arrive at a fundamental quality Carrick lacked: an ability to be streetwise when really required. For an example of Mourinho’s nous, rewind to a pre-season tour of America when this correspondent was offered an off-the-record sounding about a player he wanted out of the club but the executive did not.

The manager wanted his message out – that this was a player non grata . Machiavellian or pragmatic? A guess says Carrick would never dream of employing a similar tactic to achieve the best result for the team. But why not? Mourinho wanted a bad egg gone before the dressing room was stunk out and on-field prospects undermined.

Carrick, in his last month, encountered two of his own malevolents: Lisandro Martínez, a de facto captain who dared to criticise Wilcox’s recruitment after the 2-0 defeat by Atlético Madrid; and Bruno Fernandes, Carrick’s official leader, who betrayed his manager by questioning his tactics after the 4-1 humiliation at Como .

Each crossed a line and were emblematic of a chaotic changing room, a major factor in the dismal run of three wins from 15 games this season, including elimination from the Carabao Cup, and the league return of eight points from 10 matches that has United in the relegation zone.

Fernandes, Martínez and a club run like a banana republic are the next man’s problem, just as Mourinho inherited from Louis van Gaal, who was sacked the day after winning the 2016 FA Cup, the faults at boardroom level embodied by Woodward.

Here we see the recurring problem at United: a new gun is hired and is bequeathed a sorry mess that is impossible to clean up because there is no true will to eradicate it. Why? Because the only real reset of culture would be for Ratcliffe, who owns 29.4%, Wilcox, Berrada and the Glazer family, whose ownership since 2005 has left the club about £1.2bn in debt, to accept they are the problem and depart.

Carrick is a good guy whose adoration of United was returned to him by the support, underlined by the reception he got from the Stretford End after the 3-0 humbling by Bournemouth last month. Yet being a decent man and head coach was not enough.

In elite sport the fine margins are often trumpeted as the difference between triumph and failure. Last season, from mid-January, Carrick worked these his way as Manchester City, Arsenal, Liverpool and Chelsea were defeated and United lost only two of his 17 games as interim head coach.

This season, though, the fall-off was startling – and Carrick was found wanting. Who knows what might have occurred if United were the “best-in-class” organisation Ratcliffe insisted they would be under him. As with the muddled thinking regarding Howe, “worst in class” may be a more apt characterisation.

The agonising, overlong process to decide Carrick should be sacked was the latest illustration. On Monday evening the Guardian broke the news that Wilcox and Berrada would recommend to Ratcliffe that Carrick should be removed. Yet days passed during which Carrick still took training and it emerged the deal for Pochettino was being finalised. A proper functioning organisation would have acted more swiftly and with more style.

This is what the next manager has to grapple with. He may succeed. But the odds are stacked against it owing to the deep structural faults that undermine the modern Manchester United .

title: Denmark announced as host of 2027 UEC Road European Championships
author: cyclingnews@futurenet.com (Dani Ostanek)
text:
It's the first time the nation has hosted a major road championship since the 2017 European Championships, also held in Herning, when Alexander Kristoff and Marianne Vos raced to glory in the road races while Victor Campenaerts and Ellen van Dijk won the time trials.

Previously, the Road World Championships were held in Copenhagen, Denmark, in 2011, while the Road Worlds will head back to the nation in 2029.

Previous major championships held in Denmark have ended with mass sprint finishes, and the 2027 European Championships are also expected to favour sprinters after hilly editions in Slovenia and France in the last two years.

The 2027 UEC Road European Championships will run between September 28 and October 3, and while the exact dates of each event are not yet known, that creates a clash with La Vuelta Femenina, which begins on October 3.

"We are thrilled to be returning to Denmark after ten years. In 2017, this country hosted the second edition of the Road European Championships open to the Elite category, believing from the outset in a project that was then in its infancy," said UEC president Enrico Della Casa.

"Today, we are returning with an event that has grown considerably and has become a world-class occasion, capable of attracting the attention of the media and cycling enthusiasts from all over the world."

Hosting of the European Championships is now set for the next three years, with trips to Denmark, the North Brabant region of the Netherlands, and Abruzzo in Italy on the way.

"With Denmark in 2027, the Netherlands in 2028 and Italy, specifically the Abruzzo region, in 2029, the next three years promise to be highly prestigious for the UEC Road European Championships. These three countries, each with a deeply rooted cycling culture, demonstrate the appeal our event has gained and allow us to look to the future with great ambition," said Della Casa.

"I would like to thank the cities of Herning and Silkeborg, Sport Event Denmark, the Danish government and the Danish Cycling Federation and its President, Morten Anderson, for the trust, enthusiasm and commitment they have shown.

"Ten years ago, Denmark helped to write an important chapter in the history of our European Championships, and I am convinced that in 2027, together we will write another equally memorable one."

title: Red Bull's Lawson decision is a clean break from its Marko era
author: Edd Straw
text:
Lawson’s seat in Red Bull’s second team has been at very real risk in recent rounds, with Formula 2 race winner Nikola Tsolov waiting in the wings and Red Bull needing to decide which two of Lawson, Tsolov and Arvid Lindblad race for Racing Bulls next year.

But had Lawson lost out - with zero options elsewhere on the grid to race in 2027 - it would have been an unprecedented move.

In the past 10 seasons of F1, there have only been two comparable cases of a driver doing as well as Lawson is currently doing, getting dropped and then not having an alternative seat for the following season.

Only Sergio Perez - who was eighth in the 2024 championship - and Alex Albon - who was seventh in the 2020 championship - have been higher placed than Lawson is right now (ninth) and yet found themselves without a drive the year after.

Both, of course, met that fate thanks to Red Bull, but the big difference is both Perez and Albon were driving for Red Bull Racing - and getting absolutely destroyed by Max Verstappen in the process.

Lawson is in a completely different situation here, in that he’s the highest-placed of all midfield drivers in the 2026 world championship and comfortably ahead of his rookie team-mate Lindblad.

The main threat to Lawson’s position comes from F2 title contender Tsolov. The Bulgarian has won six races in his rookie F2 season and sits only seven points behind 2027 Haas F1 driver and Ferrari junior Rafael Camara - who made his F1 debut in place of Esteban Ocon in Brazil.

Tsolov has made a strong case for promotion, not only because of those F2 results but also because of how well he did subbing for Lawson in a mandated rookie FP1 outing in Mexico, where Tsolov lapped within two tenths of Lindblad and generally looked very at ease with the whole business of being in F1.

On top of Tsolov’s impressive showing in Mexico, Lawson later had a run-in with Red Bull’s kingpin driver Verstappen during FP2 - which earned Lawson a strong rebuke from the four-time champion, in which Verstappen alluded to Lawson’s 2027 deal uncertainty.

The Race understands the recent triple-header has basically been the crunch moment for Red Bull and Racing Bulls to do their final analysis on who should drive next year - so Lawson been under pressure during this period and at genuine risk of losing his seat.

Which perhaps explains Verstappen’s pointed remark in the wake of their collision in Mexico, “It’s just not very smart behaviour when you’re in his position to pick a fight with me.”

But the way Lawson rebounded from that low point, recovering from a technical exclusion in qualifying and a pitlane start to finish seventh that weekend, in his familiar position as the leading midfield runner, showed true grit.

Add that to the way Lawson excelled in the wet in Brazil - fifth in qualifying and seventh in the race - and it’s difficult for anyone inside the Red Bull system to make the case he should definitely be dropped.

It has only been Lawson at real risk - because Lindblad has done an excellent job alongside him as a rookie and contributed a meaningful 35% of the points that leave Racing Bulls almost certain to finish fifth in the constructors’ championship - the highest place in the team’s history.

Lawson’s job within that team is essentially to give Red Bull a benchmark of performance to measure Lindblad against. There’s no realistic possibility of Lawson becoming a contender for a Red Bull Racing seat again, in the way there might still be for Lindblad or, eventually, Tsolov.

The trouble is that Lawson has done such an excellent job in his role this season - and has even taken a further step as a driver since subbing for Isack Hadjar at Red Bull for three races - that he made himself impossible to drop even though his presence no longer really fits the 'Red Bull conveyor belt' function Racing Bulls is supposed to have.

On Friday in Brazil, Racing Bulls team boss Alan Permane said Racing Bulls is trying to “apply a little bit of science” to the situation, a clear rebuke of the days when Helmut Marko would hire and fire junior drivers seemingly almost on a whim.

“Red Bull's had a very successful young driver programme, and if I want to be... and I don't want to be critical of it, but I think if you guys are critical of it, maybe sometimes the drivers haven't been able to have enough time to settle, or maybe some snap decisions have been made,” Permane said.

Lawson’s average qualifying advantage over Lindblad is only seven hundredths of a second, but in the races - where the points are paid out - Lawson has a clear advantage.

He’s scored in 13 of the 17 grands prix he’s started for Racing Bulls this year, as well as taking points in three of the six sprint races staged. He’s also finished ahead of Lindblad 11 times out of the 14 races they have both finished and run ahead of him on 77% of the racing laps both completed.

That’s made him the undisputed king of the midfield. Of the 52 qualifying sessions and races, including sprints, held this year, Lawson has been classified at the top of that group 18 times.

To put that number in context, remember Alpine and Audi have made the fight at the front of that group a close one, and that Lawson wasn’t part of the midfield for eight of those because he was in Hadjar’s Red Bull.

His approach has also caught the eye. Prior to 2026, there were times when his decision-making in battle could be self-defeating. That led to more on-track incidents than necessary.

That’s something he’s largely cut out this year, while still fighting hard enough to get the results.

He’s also adapted well to the 2026 cars, recognising he needed to contain the desire to over-drive to get the most out of them - not easy to do for a driver who can be naturally aggressive on corner entries.

He’s also able to piece together weekends consistently well, often turning things round even if they start badly on Friday.He also did a good job in those three outings for Red Bull, despite the scars of what happened to him in 2025. That shows a mental robustness, which is also reflected in his mindset amid uncertainty about his future. He’s been able to focus on doing his job and not been distracted by this - something that is easier said than done.

Lawson explained: “A year ago I thought about it a lot. It was very much in my head and you just drive worse when you overthink things.”

Lawson hasn’t suddenly transformed himself into the best driver in F1. But he’s taken a big step to become a rounded, consistent, and dependable midfield performer - and a very quick one too.

That’s what eventually made him undroppable for 2027.

Permane had already suggested “everyone will be happy” when the announcement finally came, so that suggests that now Lawson has been confirmed alternative arrangements will be made for Tsolov - which will most likely mean an official reserve driver role and an expanded programme of F1 testing and free practice running in 2027.

title: Racing Bulls officially keeps Lawson for 2027
author: Jon Noble
text:
Liam Lawson will remain at Racing Bulls next season after the squad announced an unchanged Formula 1 line-up for 2027.

The New Zealander’s future had been uncertain for many weeks, with the Red Bull-owned outfit pondering whether to keep him on alongside Arvid Lindblad or promote its junior driver Nikola Tsolov.

However, as reported earlier this week, Lawson’s recent strong performances in Mexico and Brazil were understood to have put him on course for a new deal and convinced Racing Bulls he was the best candidate.

With Lawson currently sitting ninth in the drivers’ standings, as best of the rest behind the top four teams, and his contribution key to helping Racing Bulls sit fifth in the constructors’ championship, it would have been nonsensical to have dropped him.

Racing Bulls team principal Alan Permane believed that the line-up of Lawson and Lindblad was the perfect one in terms of blending youth and experience.

“Both have demonstrated their ability and potential throughout the season, and we’ve seen the progress they’ve made, both individually and as a pairing,” explained Permane.

“I have no doubt that this is the best driver line-up for us, bringing a strong combination of experience and ambition. Together, we have a solid foundation to build on the progress made this year, continue pushing ourselves forward and take the next step towards achieving our ambitions in 2027."

Lawson has earned praise in the paddock this year for his standout performances for both Racing Bulls and during a stand-in run at Red Bull, when he filled in for the injured Isack Hadjar.

He thanked Racing Bulls for the belief in him.

“We've had a brilliant season together and the team has worked very hard to produce a fast car, which I've loved driving,” he said.

“It feels great to be part of a historic season for the team as we continue our fight for P5 in the constructors' championship.

"It's a testament to the hard work of everyone both at track, and back at the factory. I’m looking forward to carrying this momentum forward with Arvid through to 2027; we're building something super positive and I’m excited by what we can achieve together.”

The Racing Bulls statement that announced Lawson and Lindblad were staying for 2027 did not make any reference to plans for Tsolov, who is in the hunt to clinch the F2 crown this year.

The Bulgarian had a rookie FP1 run for Racing Bulls in Mexico, and will likely have a wider role with Red Bull in 2027. He has also been linked with a switch to Super Formula in Japan.

title: UK economy grows at fastest rate for more than two years
text:
﻿The UK economy grew at its fastest rate for more than two years in the three months to September.

Between July and September, the economy expanded by 0.7%, accelerating from the three months previously, official figures show.

The robust growth suggests a far more resilient economy than expected over the summer.

Strong growth in the services sector - which includes non-physical goods such as consultancy services and hotels and restaurants - helped drive the stronger growth.

Within services, computer programming registered its fastest growth for the past three years, helped by AI linked spending.

The boost from computer programming and consultancy services has been the biggest driver of growth so far this year.

Grant Fitzner, chief economist at the Office for National Statistics, said it was "possible growth could have been even stronger" if there hadn't been a war in the Middle East.

But he says households may not feel better off as a result with inflation and wages figures having a more direct impact on people.

"Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the figures were "welcome news".

He said: "Despite a year where events around the world have pushed up costs here at home, our economy is growing, bringing hope for the future.

The latest figures put the UK on course to be the second fastest growing economy across the major G7 countries which also includes Canada, Japan, Germany, Italy and France.

However, Jake Finney, senior economist at consultancy PwC, cautioned that growth was likely to slow over the coming months "unless energy markets stabilise".

A sharp rise in energy bills is forecast for January, which is likely to hit consumer spending and confidence, he said.

Richard Benc, who founded mechanical watch company Studio Underdog, five years ago as a passion project during Covid, says sales are better than he expected.

"We've seen more resilience than we had forecast for and expected. We are still projecting growth this year," he says.

The business exports about 80% of its watches. "We've seen a surprising amount of resilience, particularly from our US customers. We have also seen resilience in our UK buyers," he says, although some UK customers are now taking longer to buy watches."

title: 'No serious damage' – Lucinda Brand escapes serious injury following her crash at the Niel Superprestige
author: Owen Rogers
text:
After initially fearing the worst, Lucinda Brand was not seriously injured when she hit the barrier during the Superprestige Jaarmarktcross cyclo-cross race at Niel on Wednesday.

Early on during round three of the season-long Superprestige series, World Champion Brand briefly lost control of her bike, hitting the barrier and twisting her ankle as she put her foot down.

Despite what was apparently an innocuous incident, her discomfort was clear immediately; the 37-year-old first grimaced, then fell into tears, before abandoning the race she had hoped to win for a fifth time.

After the incident, her Baloise Verzekeringen-Het Poetsbureau Lions team manager, former World Champion Sven Nys, was fearful Brand had suffered a severe injury , telling Play Sport: "If Lucinda has tears in her eyes, that is usually not a good sign. She is quite a tough cookie, which is why I am a bit worried now."

Then, in a post on the team’s Instagram account, he added: "She can’t put force on her foot right now, so I think it’s important that we monitor that and make sure that nothing was damaged.

"Hoping we won’t lose her for the rest of the season."

However, Nys has since been reassured. "Everything is okay. No serious damage was detected; she just needs to make sure it doesn’t happen again. Taping the foot is important now, though," he told Belgian paper .

The season continues apace this weekend, and Brand would have been expected to start round four of the Superprestige at Merkplas on Saturday and Sunday’s Bollekesccross, the second round of the X2O Badkamers Trofee, a series she leads, after winning the Koppenbergcross, and which she has won on four previous occasions. However, following her injury, Brand’s participation is yet to be confirmed.

title: Sepp Kuss Eats Cookies for Breakfast and Is Embarrassed by Trophies. He’s Pro Cycling’s Hero Next Door.
author: Jim Cotton
text:
(Photo: OSCAR DEL POZO/AFP via Getty Images)

Sepp Kuss could just be the dude next door who’s good at riding bikes.

In a new “Day in the Life” video, Kuss walks viewers through the boring mundanity of his life at home in Andorra during the off-season.

As you’d expect from Colorado’s fan favorite, it’s all pretty chill.

There are cookies for breakfast, grand tour trophies gathering dust in hallways, and a man-cave cluttered with bike bits.

His lifestyle seems hilariously lackadaisical. His home has few trappings of an elite athlete who’s likely getting paid seven figures.

The high-end Porsche parked in the garage is the one giveaway that this is not your normal guy.

Visma-Lease a Bike released its “Day in the Life” mini-doc this week after its long-signed American star blasted through one of his best seasons yet.

This year, Kuss rode all three grand tours in the season for the second time in his career.

The “Eagle of Durango” won a stage at the Giro d’Italia, nearly won two stages at the Tour de France, and made a late surge for fifth overall at the Vuelta a España.

Few riders dare take on three grand tours in a season, but Kuss made it look easy.

In the video, Kuss says the program keeps life how he likes it – simple and stress-free.

“I’ve been able to be home a lot between all three grand tours [this year], and that makes a big difference,” he says.

“Mentally it was easier than a normal season, because you have really concrete blocks and concrete goals. Between that, it’s a pretty simple routine and easy living,” he says.

Kuss’ young family is no doubt front of mind when he structures his calendar.

His Spanish-born wife, Noemi, and two-year-old daughter, Martina, feature heavily in the documentary, and Sepp is in all-out dad-mode throughout.

He plays with his daughter, takes her on a bike ride, and helps Noemi feed her bits of cake.

Kuss is pro cycling’s ultimate dad next door.

He’s just a 32-year-old dude who casually enjoys bikes, baking, and crushing Tour de France climbs at a billion watts per kilo.

And yes, you read that right, Kuss appears to be a passionate baker – one with a sweet tooth.

Food and food-prep feature heavily in the show.

There’s no controversial kimchi-and-gnocchi concoction like the one favored by Matteo Jorgenson, but there are some interesting insights.

Kuss reveals a refreshingly casual attitude to food that’s careful but far from restrictive.

“Every morning has to start with cookies or a cake,” Kuss says as he cuts the final slices of what looks like a huge home bake.

“We usually try to go for something more homemade, but a lot of the time it’s just normal cookies from the grocery store. Not a perfect diet,” he smiles.

The waifish climber adds that he barely restricts and allows a little luxury, all year round.

It’s no doubt all carefully considered and meticulously tracked on a food app, but Kuss doesn’t appear overly concerned about optimizing his W/Kg ratio in the depths of off-season.

“My diet is never so strict. It stays pretty much the same all year,” he says. “We eat well, but there’s nothing that I don’t eat in the off-season versus in the normal season.

“There are always some chips in the pantry,” he adds.

Kuss’s “aww shucks” character and boyish charm have made him one of the darlings of the pro peloton.

He’s well liked by his colleagues, loved by the media (he’ll rarely say no to an interview), and adored by fans.

Kuss’ reluctant stardom is epitomized as the camera follows him through his home.

Bike mementos are casually scattered in random places and seemingly displayed out of obligation.

The huge wine bottle he won at the Giro d’Italia is gathering dust in a doorway.

His Vuelta a España stage-winner’s plaque sits on a shelf in the garage alongside a handmade #GCKuss token and a bunch of random bike oils.

“You either have a trophy room, or you find the nice ones to put somewhere, but …,” Kuss says with a shy shrug.

Kuss’ garage also functions as a bike store and workshop.

Unlike the many pros who can barely change a tire, Kuss is teaching himself the art of bike maintenance as a “hobby mechanic.”

Oh, and the special-edition red Cervélo that Kuss rode on the final stage of his career-crowning ride at the Vuelta?

Lost in a mess of a half-dozen bikes hanging in a rack.

What did you expect? A pride-of-place position hanging on the wall of his lounge?

Kuss is one of the greatest U.S. racers of his generation.

He became the first North American to win a grand tour in a decade when he won the 2023 Vuelta a España, and is one of the few active pros to have taken a stage at all three of cycling’s three-week races.

But Kuss often seems embarrassed by his own success.

It should be considered a miracle then, that his Vuelta a España winner’s trophy has made it out of the cupboard.

The large circular prize he was awarded in 2023 stands on a cabinet in a dark corner of his home.

And that low-key position should be considered progress.

Last year, Kuss revealed in a Sigma Sport video that his prestigious trophy wasn’t proudly standing triumphant in a cabinet, but tucked deep in the back of a cupboard.

Visma’s recently retired Dutch stalwart Robert Gesink makes a cameo appearance in the video when he meets Kuss for a coffee.

The 40-year-old believes Kuss’ innate zen has bought him longevity.

“The biggest strength of Sepp is that he found the really nice balance,” Gesink says. “He does everything right, he weighs his food, he does his training correctly, but he has the right balance and doesn’t overdo it.

“If you can keep that balance and find a way that works for you and you can sustain that level, then you can keep growing,” Gesink continues.

“That’s how you can build such a long and successful career if you find your own way to make that sustainable and not lose yourself straight away in all these little details.”

Kuss is currently out in L.A. visiting Cervélo HQ with several Visma-Lease a Bike teammates.…

title: 'I don't get often very emotional' – Tadej Pogačar highlights a teammate's Tour de France stage win as 'one of the best days of my career'
author: Patrick Fletcher
text:
Tadej Pogačar has no shortage of highlights from his eight years so far as a professional bike racer but he has picked out a teammate’s victory as "one of the best days of my career".

"The first stages, nine, was really nice," Pogačar says from a massage table, presumably after stage nine as he talks about it being “super hot” and references "three victories" taken by the team.

"I think the one that Isaac wins, in Barcelona, I got also really emotional, and I don’t get often very emotional," Pogačar says.

"So, one of the best days of my career," he adds.

The comments are brief but striking in the context of all that Pogačar has won, including five Tour de France titles, 26 Tour de France stages of his own, 13 Monument Classics, and two world titles.

For all the talk of his insatiable appetite for victory, he seemingly took just as much joy in sacrificing the chance of another one and helping someone else, who may one day come to rival him.

And it wasn’t just that day in Barcelona; with a commanding lead in the yellow jersey Pogačar went on to effectively work as a domestique for Del Toro again and again in the second half of the Tour de France, notably on the stage 15 summit finish at Plateau de Solaison and on the penultimate day to Alpe d’Huez when Del Toro’s podium position came under fire from Paul Seixas.

"You try to be the best version of yourself but we don’t know how we are perceived in the third person," Del Toro said in a recent interview with Spanish newspaper in reference to Pogačar’s treatment of him.

"That he can see something that maybe I’m not seeing is flattering, but also quite something. He wants to be part of my process and support me in each opportunity. It’s something very beautiful and I feel very privileged."

title: Michael Carrick sacked by Manchester United with Pochettino poised to take over
author: Jamie Jackson and Pablo Iglesias Maurer
text:
Club pay tribute to ‘legend’ but say change ‘necessary’

Pochettino in line to take two USA games before leaving

Mauricio Pochettino is poised to sign a deal to take over at Manchester United after Michael Carrick was sacked as the head coach with the team in the Premier League’s ­relegation zone.

Pochettino was on Thursday discussing the final details to join a club with one win from their past 11 matches. He will lead the USA for the last time in their Concacaf Nations League quarter-final games against Haiti on Saturday and on Tuesday and should be at Carrington next week to prepare United to face Liverpool at Anfield in their first match after the international break. With the second US game finishing in the early hours of Wednesday GMT, his first day with United is expected to be Thursday.

United have been in contact with US Soccer to extricate Pochettino from a contract that runs to 2030. The former Southampton, Tottenham and Chelsea manager has a release clause of about $10m (£7.5m) and United will have to pay more to take his staff.

Carrick’s departure comes with United third from bottom of the Premier League, a point behind 17th-placed Coventry, and 17th in the Champions League standings. It follows a review led by the ­director of football, Jason Wilcox, and a ­recommendation to Sir Jim Ratcliffe, who controls sporting policy. Wilcox and United’s chief executive, Omar ­Berrada, travelled to Monaco to meet Ratcliffe .

Carrick’s sacking was then signed off at a board meeting involving the Glazer family. Carrick turned up for work on Thursday morning – as he has done each day this week – with his fate in effect sealed. No further training will be held until next week.

United said: “After a disappointing start to the season, the club has come to the extremely difficult conclusion that a change is necessary in order to achieve our ambitions. Michael is, and always will be, a Manchester United legend. Just as he did as a player, he has conducted himself with the highest standards of ­dedication and professionalism throughout his time back with the club. His leadership and achievements last season will always be fondly remembered.”

Eddie Howe, out of a job since leaving Newcastle in July , had been on Wilcox’s radar as a replacement for Carrick, while the former Germany and Bayern Munich coach Julian Nagelsmann was the initial choice of Christopher Vivell, the director of recruitment. But United have targeted Pochettino, who left Chelsea in May 2024 and took the USA job four months later .

Carrick was given the job in May on a contract to 2028 after a successful interim spell during which he secured Champions League qualification. He won 12 and drew three of his 17 games last season, but has been unable to continue that trend.

United have three victories so far this season in all competitions – at home to Ipswich, Sabah and Roma. They twice fought back from two goals down last Sunday to salvage a late point in a 4-4 home draw with Aston Villa , after a dramatic recovery to beat Roma 3-2 , but the club concluded a change was needed.

Carrick was allowed three games after a 3-0 home defeat by Bournemouth to prove he remained the right person for the job, but United felt after the performances against Chelsea , where they lost 2-0, Roma (won 3-2) and Villa (4-4) that they were on the wrong path and that another coach could get far more from the squad. They consider 18th place in the Premier League unacceptable.

The sacking continues a period of turmoil at United also marked by Bruno Fernandes challenging Carrick’s strategy after a 4-1 Champions League defeat at Como and Lisandro Martínez criticising Wilcox.

Since Sir Alex Ferguson left in 2013 the club have appointed eight managers, including Ralf Rangnick, who had a five-month interim spell. Carrick is the second head coach fired by United in one calendar year, after Ruben Amorim went in January, a first for the club.

title: The chaos that took Carrick from two-year deal to sacked within 15 games
text:
It was just after 6pm on Sunday, 8 November when the message landed. Manchester United were 4-2 down to Aston Villa, and Old Trafford was resigned to defeat.

The plea came from someone who knows Michael Carrick well, has worked with him and understands at first hand the pressures of life in the United goldfish bowl.

As it turned out, the predicted ending did not come to pass.

United scored twice in stoppage time to salvage a 4-4 draw. Carrick celebrated Patrick Dorgu's equaliser by raising an arm in the air. After that, he walked round the pitch on what has turned out to be a final lap of appreciation.

As the United supporters sang his name, Carrick placed himself in the middle of his players to ensure the fans did not turn on them in the way they had done after the 3-0 defeat by Bournemouth two weeks before.

It was a decision that summed up the 45-year-old - supporting the collective, rather than looking after himself.

That obvious desire to do the best for his club and his players - and his storied past - explains why Carrick's song continued to be bellowed from the stands when just about everyone else involved at United was attracting fury and derision.

To get this far is longer than many envisaged. It seemed there was no way Carrick could survive the Bournemouth debacle.

United took 44 hours to communicate to the wider world they were sticking with him then, though it is understood Carrick was told the day before.

Since then, it has been chaos. United have won one, drawn one and lost one.

Outstanding in the opening 45 minutes at Chelsea, they conceded at the start of the second half before defender Lisandro Martinez was sent off for two bookings in the space of five minutes. They lost 2-0.

Awful and two goals down inside 17 minutes against Roma in the Champions League, they roared back with the kind of thrilling comeback Carrick was part of so often during Sir Alex Ferguson's days to win 3-2.

Then, Villa. Two goals down in four minutes thanks to calamitous goalkeeping, they clawed back to level before half-time. More abysmal defending left United with another mountain to climb - but they emerged from the carnage with a point.

Try picking the bones out of that. Had Carrick's stock increased, or had it merely proven he was not the right man the job? United decided it was the latter.

Chief executive Omar Berrada and director of football Jason Wilcox celebrated Dorgu's stoppage-time equaliser against Villa in the directors' box. But they had a slightly detached perspective.

Within days they were flying to Monaco to tell minority owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe change was required.

For the third season in a row, United are replacing the man in charge of the team mid-season.

Unlike with Erik ten Hag and Ruben Amorim, this decision is not a surprise. Not because of what is happening now, but because what is happening now is so at odds with what happened last season.

After 12 wins in 17 games under Carrick and a return to the Champions League, the mood in pre-season was overwhelmingly positive.

There were no signs of splits, young players including JJ Gabriel were part of the group, and senior staff spoke optimistically about the potential of Bruno Fernandes' proposed partnership with Youri Tielemans.

Recruitment was clearly an issue, but more of that later.

Looking back, the 48 hours before United's season-opening match at Hull were pivotal.

With Benjamin Sesko still trying to ease his way back from the shin issue that ended his previous campaign early, Amad Diallo suffered an ankle injury that would rule him out for seven weeks. It meant Carrick was deprived of his first-choice striking alternative, with Bryan Mbeumo having to play on the right of the attack.

Carrick instead turned to Matheus Cunha, whose preference for dropping deep took him into the spaces captain Fernandes likes to occupy.

It neutralised United's attack on a day they seemed ill-prepared to meet the physical challenge of an opponent motivated by their long-awaited Premier League return.

In his role as interviewer for Nordic broadcaster Viaplay, former Norway and Middlesbrough striker Jan Aage Fjortoft claimed United had lacked passion - something Carrick dismissed as "ridiculous".

"It's one game," Carrick told the media afterwards.

The following week, United were losing to Ipswich - another newly promoted side. Only a slip from Marcelino Nunez inside his own half allowed Cunha to tee up Fernandes for an undeserved equaliser. Fernandes, who had just been crowned PFA Player of the Year for 2025-26, went on to complete a hat-trick in a 5-2 win.

United have not won in the Premier League since.

After that came a trip to Everton. Twice United led, the second time when Sesko struck two minutes from time after coming on as a substitute. Deep into stoppage time, Ainsley Maitland-Niles drove home from long range to deny the visitors.

Asked how confident he was in his side's ability to react to a disappointing start to the season, Carrick snapped back: "It's not been that bad."

Time and again, United's fitness was called into question. They struggled badly against a Manchester City side reduced to 10 men in the first half before City benefited from an Erling Haaland goal that referees' chief Howard Webb later admitted should not have stood.

Carrick's complaints after the match were justified - but they masked a poor performance from his team.

After taking a 2-0 lead inside 10 minutes against Brighton in the EFL Cup, United were outplayed and beaten, thanks to two goals in four second-half minutes.

Carrick's coaching staff - lauded months earlier - could not find an answer.

The head coach said Cunha's injury-time equaliser against a Fulham side who started the game bottom was a positive to build on. But immediately after the international break, United were held to another draw - conceding in injury time to an out-of-form and 10-man Tottenham.

The familiar downward spiral was getting out of control.…

title: Russell launches fully-funded new karting academy
author: Fleur Mealing
text:
Mercedes Formula 1 driver George Russell has launched a new karting academy at Silverstone aimed at developing the next generation of motorsport talent, with 25 young drivers set to receive a fully funded championship opportunity in 2027.

The GR63 Karting Academy will be open to boys and girls aged eight and nine, with Russell hoping to provide a route into motorsport for talented youngsters who might otherwise be held back by the financial demands of the sport.

Based at Silverstone's karting circuit, the initiative will run across four stages, beginning with open-access qualifying sessions in December 2026.

The first stage will see eligible drivers compete in arrive-and-drive sessions between December 6 and 31, with the 80 fastest progressing to a shootout on January 31, 2027.

From there, 25 drivers will be selected for the GR63 Championship, an eight-round series running from March to November 2027. Each round will take place on a different circuit configuration at Silverstone, with all participation costs covered by the academy.

The 25 selected drivers will also receive a full set of academy equipment, including racing overalls, a helmet, gloves and boots.

The programme will culminate in December 2027, when the championship's top five finishers compete in a final race at Silverstone. Drivers will be evaluated on their talent, lap times, fitness, racecraft and media skills, with the overall winner receiving a fully-funded karting season in 2028.

Russell will help mentor and guide participants throughout the programme.

"Karting is where it all started for me, and it taught me everything I've relied on throughout my career," said Russell.

"I know how hard it is for talented young drivers to get that first opportunity, especially when budgets are tight.

"With the GR63 Karting Academy, I want to give something back by finding those hidden talents and giving them the support and platform they need to reach their potential."

The financial accessibility of the programme is a central part of its appeal. While the initial qualifying sessions will cost £25 and entry to the January shootout will cost £75, everything from the championship stage onwards will be fully funded.

The initiative is being supported by Silverstone and the British Racing Drivers' Club (BRDC), with BRDC president David Coulthard welcoming the opportunity to invest in Britain's motorsport future.

"The GR63 Academy captures that ethos perfectly, and we are delighted to work with George to support the next generation of drivers here at Silverstone," said Coulthard.

How to enter the GR63 Karting Academy

The initial arrive-and-drive qualifying sessions will take place at Silverstone Kart Track between December 6 and 31, 2026, at a cost of £25.

All applicants must be citizens of a Commonwealth country.

title: Why Mercedes cannot dominate F1's new era
author: Jon Noble
text:
They say history doesn't repeat itself, but it often rhymes. And that applies to Formula 1 as well.

The start of new-rules eras have often been hugely indicative of what is to come, as the trends of the inaugural season lay down the story of future years.

If we do some comparisons of the first years of the most recent major rules-change eras, we can see how the comparisons between the first and second half of each of those seasons gave us a hint of what was to come in the following campaigns.

In 2009, Brawn GP took the crowns thanks to its stellar start to the year, but you could see Red Bull getting its act together ahead of what became its era of dominance.

In 2014, Mercedes was unstoppable and its advantage through the year clearly told us about it becoming the main force in F1.

In 2022, Ferrari started well but Red Bull got the weight off its car and pushed forward to begin Max Verstappen's real run of supremacy, off the back of his maiden title the year before.

For 2026, Mercedes has secured both crowns, but the story of the year is an intriguing one because a trend has emerged of there being no clear benchmark late on.

While Kimi Antonelli and George Russell kicked 2026 off strongly and laid title-winning foundations early on, subsequent spells of success for Red Bull, McLaren and Ferrari have pointed to a shift.

In fact, as the table below shows, if you take the results of the last five races up until and including Brazil, Mercedes is only the third-highest-scoring team.

Last five total points: 92Overall total: 398 (4tth)

F1 has a super-close top four where no team seems to have been able to edge clear of its rivals, and it has been hard to pick out anyone who has built up some momentum.

This is why, for all the joy that Mercedes team principal Toto Wolff has taken from getting his team back to title-winning ways, he has no sense that this is the start of "runaway" success.

"It looks like the most competitive era that is about to start," he said.

"The teams have become so professional in capability and resource that these kind of runaway seasons, I don't see them anymore, whether it's four in a row or eight in a row. And that is a completely new challenge.

"You can see how quickly it goes from you being dominant and within a few races you realise that your upgrade doesn't work and you fall back and you're just third on the road. So it's great for the sport.

"I wish it was the era of Mercedes and me running away with another few championships. I don't think it's the reality."

The upgrade war seems to have had the effect of repeatedly shuffling the order of the top four.

Whenever any of the major teams have brought big development steps, often those have helped push them to the front and changed the hierarchy.

McLaren team principal Andrea Stella has labelled this "ping pong season" in terms of how teams bounce between being at the front or the back of that top-four block.

"Anybody that upgrades kind of takes an advantage, but even if you do a good job of developing, not necessarily [is it the case that] you can establish yourself at the top," he said recently.

"We have a variable level of supremacy, dependent on the track conditions or the optimisation of the set-up.

"But the reality is that I think nowhere before we have had F1 so competitive and with such a rate of development. If we raced with the race-one car [from the Australia season opener], we will be one and a half seconds slower than what we are at the moment."

The cause of this major shuffling is not only the fact that the big teams all seem to be so evenly matched in terms of their capability. (And have found ways to all keep pushing on with developments under the cost cap.)

It is that the FIA appears to have made life very difficult for teams because the aero regulations are so restrictive, leaving designers with only very small areas they can work on.

Focused on creating cars that did not produce significant dirty air, the FIA was determined not to allow areas that teams could exploit to ruin this and improve downforce.

And this has left teams capped in terms of how much performance they have been able to eke out.

Stella added: "If you take the regulations and you define the volumes within which you can put aerodynamic devices, that's not how an aerodynamicist would do it.

"They [the rules] have been done in a certain way somehow to jeopardise for the sake of competition and also for the sake of allowing the following and the overtaking."

Red Bull team principal Laurent Mekies agreed on the lack of design freedom leading to diminishing returns for all teams.

"The convergence is probably happening earlier than what we all thought," he said. "I'm guessing somehow, it's perhaps an indication of fairly restrictive regulations.

"That being said, you see cars with visibly different concepts and you see four top teams fighting, which is probably a great point to be for the sport.

"So, let's see how it will pan out in the second year. But to be already in the second part of '26 in situations where you turn up at the race weekend and you don't know which one of the four top teams is going to win the race, I think it's great for the sport."

The end result of all this is a form book that is in a state of flux.

Ferrari team principal Fred Vasseur thought that the 'ping pong' element of rapidly shuffling fortunes was a consequence of immature rules offering potential for big gains, something that will slow down into next season where he felt teams would converge more.

"Each time that we were bringing something, we are doing a step," he said. "That was a little bit the story of the season because, as we [the top-four teams] were not bringing upgrades at the same races, you have this kind of rotation.

"Probably it could be less through next year and the following years, but we will have a kind of convergence of performance of where we are next year."

And it's for this reason that Wolff was convinced that it is important Mercedes gets back to its early performance levels now that give it a springboard into next year.

"Look at the last few races: we haven't won [Mercedes has one win in the last five]," he said in Brazil.

"The competition has been getting tougher, between Ferrari, McLaren, Red Bull and ourselves. It's four teams that can win races and will be challenging for a world championship. And I have no doubt that it's going to be very difficult for us next year.

"For me, the 2027 season has started now."

title: Thursday briefing: What we do (and don’t) know about Alice Huang and the Nvidia affair

title: Freddie Slater's 'surreal' first taste of Formula 1
text:
While Kimi Antonelli was making history as the youngest Formula 1 world champion earlier this month, a British teenager was taking his own steps to a glittering career in the sport.

Freddie Slater made his debut in the free practice sessions at both the Mexican and Sao Paulo Grand Prix.

Slater, who grew up in Stratford-upon-Avon and was educated in Bromsgrove, was handed his first official F1 outing by Audi, and the 18-year-old is one of Britain's brightest motorsport prospects.

He has so far had successful seasons in karting and cars, most recently finishing runner up in the Formula 3 Championship, and told the BBC his latest experiences were "surreal".

"You're doing 350kph (217mph) into turn one at Mexico, I've never done anything like it, honestly it's just incredible," he said.

"(In) 2023, I was still in karting, then last year I was in the Formula Regional Championship which I won, and this year Formula 3."

Formula 3 is a support series organised by the FIA and competes alongside Formula 1, visiting the same tracks and racing on the same weekends.

It's an opportunity for drivers to get themselves noticed and for Slater it allowed him to become the first driver to be signed to Audi's driver development programme.

That has led to the recent outings in the team's Formula 1 cars.

"It's been great to have the support of Audi and the support of people like team principal Mattia Binotto and racing director Allan McNish.

"I didn't expect this opportunity to come so early if I'm honest. I just love speed and sitting in that F1 car was just the most surreal and incredible feeling. I've waited my whole life for this.

"I think the big difference with the F1 paddock is the amount of people, you have hundreds of people behind you, to get that car on track."

Slater's time in the car was cut short on both occasions due to mechanical problems - not uncommon for teams in practice sessions because both the driver and teams are learning the track and what setup works best. He adds that the opportunity itself to drive an F1 car was a dream come true.

"Honestly, I couldn't believe it when I was told I was getting to drive... it was just incredible getting those laps behind me with the forces and speeds involved".

Racing from a young age meant balancing exams and coursework with travelling around the world.

Slater's former headmaster, Mike Marie at Bromsgrove Preparatory School, said: "We're so proud of Freddie after having his first practice at an F1 weekend. My memories of Freddie were of him coming into school in year four with trophies bigger than he was, always incredibly talented, we wish him the best of luck on the world stage."

Slater recalls his time at school and the support he received there fondly: "I had to take prolonged absences to go racing, but also the friendships I've built up, the effort I put in at a young age."

Slater's family still live in Warwickshire and he is the oldest of five children.

"I love coming home after a busy race weekend, it's nice to unwind away from the pressure of the paddock, but also to catch up with family and friends.

"Motorsport is in my family, my dad used to race himself, my two brothers are also climbing the ladder, the youngest of which is 10 and just started karting."

Slater will now be gearing up for a season in Formula 2 with Invicta Racing, the current championship leaders. It means he will be around the paddock more often on a grand prix weekend - an opportunity he is relishing.

"Getting to Formula 1 is super difficult because the margins are so small and the drivers are at the top of their game.

"Of course I want to win a championship, that's got to be the goal every year, but it's also to develop as a driver.

"It's a tough sport in terms of how long the years are, there is so much testing, and training, that's the side people don't see."

Slater is not due on-track again until next year, however he will still be putting in the hours on the simulator and hitting the gym on a daily basis to stay fit.

With the support of Audi, he is also likely to feature in another practice session in the not-too-distant future.

text:
In 2022 and 2023, Hartshead Moor East, near Leeds, was voted the worst in Great Britain. Ever since, staff have been on a mission to redeem its reputation

In October 2023, at Skelton Lake service station on the M1 south-east of Leeds, Janine Gray received some bad news. She was surrounded by journalists and leading lights from the transport industry: people from the AA, the RAC, motorway service area chief executives, officials from National Highways. The big dogs. And it was among these gathered dignitaries that Gray heard the news she had been hoping, for the previous 12 months, not to hear. For the second year running, Hartshead Moor East – one half of the motorway services near Leeds that she managed – had been officially declared the worst service station in Britain.

This poll, conducted annually by the consumer watchdog Transport Focus, always makes the news. It produces gags on Have I Got News For You, punning headlines in the papers, “and finally” segments on local TV channels. Now Gray and her staff would be subjected to another round of ridicule. Of all the country’s service stations, which have a sort of aura of shitness to them anyway, theirs was apparently the shittest. Again.

title: Cavaliers 115, Knicks 107: Scenes from a wide free throw gap
author: Russell Richardson
text:
Four nights ago, in Cleveland, the Knicks beat the Cavaliers by 12 points thanks to dominant second and third quarters. Tonight, as we saluted our veterans, the two teams squared up once more, this time at Madison Square Garden. Yet again, our heroes dropped the first frame, but won the second, tied the third, and managed to tie the game midway through the fourth. The Cavs were determined not to let this one slip through their fingers, and with season-highs for two of ’em, James Harden (32 PTS, 9-14 FG) and Tyrese Proctor (15 PTS), they sealed the win in the final minutes, 115-107.

With his eleventh double-double, Karl-Anthony Towns (21 PTS, 11 RBS, 7-11 FG) tied Willis Reed for the longest double-double streak to start a Knicks season. They shot better from the floor and in the paint, but the guests attempted 14 more free throws. It didn’t help that New York surrendered 19 points off turnovers.

Last week, Peyton Watson (7 PTS) took most of Cleveland’s shots to start the game. This time, Kenny Atkinson’s club leveled its attack. Their defense hummed, too, with Evan Mobley (10 PTS, 5 RBS) and Watson swatting down shots, and Donovan Mitchell (23 PTS) and Harden picking pockets. Benchman Proctor led the team with eight points in the quarter, while Watson crashed the boards and spread out dimes. Jarrett Allen, who missed last week’s contest, cleared five early boards and finished with an 11-14 double-double.

Josh Hart (6 PTS, 26 MIN), back in the lineup after missing three games (ankle, illness), surely had nothing to do with the Knicks’ starters dragging their heels. Jalen Brunson (27 PTS, 12-23 FG) and OG Anunoby (14 PTS) were the only Knicks with points until Mohamed Diawara checked in midway through the frame and scored. Mitchell picked on the sophomore, dribbled around him, and burned him with a fadeaway.

The hometown club converted 25% of its first eight longball tries and attempted no free throws in the first frame. Strange but true. Towns, Brunson, and Shamet had the hot hands early, while Mikal Bridges, Josh Hart, and Andre Drummond combined to shoot 0-for-6 in the first half. Bridges would usually defend Mitchell, but Brown assigned Shamet to him. You can feel the coach’s confidence waning, no?

The Ohio Players hit nine straight shots, led by as many as 12, and won the quarter, 33–23.

We weren’t sweating the first quarter. New York dropped the first period by one in their previous matchup. Tonight, they opened the second on a 9–1 run behind Towns, Shamet, and Tyler Kolek. The latter hit two buckets and was a team-high plus-eight as the good guys climbed back into the game. Towns was cooking, too, scoring 13 points in his first 13 minutes, grabbing seven boards, and stuffing Allen’s shot. Miles McBride hit three threes in under two minutes, including the one that erased the last of a 12-point deficit and knotted the game at 43.

Brunson splashed a go-ahead three, but Harden answered with two of his own, Mitchell hit his freebies, and Mobley dunked to push Cleveland’s lead back to six. Mike Brown tried to give Towns a breather and watched the Knicks’ progress evaporate without him. KAT jumped back in and dunked with authority.

During the period, Brunson reached 11,000 career points, 3,000 assists, and 1,000 three-pointers. He’s one of seven active players in that club, along with LeBron James, Harden, Damian Lillard, Devin Booker, Luka Dončić, and Trae Young. Congratulations, Cap!

At halftime, the guests were ahead 59–53. Harden led all scorers with 17 (5-of-7 FG), while KAT topped the Knicks with 15. Bizarrely, New York took a single free throw all half, and Cleveland’s seven extra points at the line more than covered the margin. Both teams made 22 field goals (52% for Cleveland, 51% for New York) and grabbed 17 boards apiece. Cleveland had a 26–20 edge in the paint, but New York shot 40% from three to the Cavs’ 37% and scored one more point from the field.

Cleveland opened the third on a 10–5 run, with threes from Watson, Mitchell, and Harden stretching the lead to 69–58. Spida missed his next two threes and picked up a charge. From there, the hosts got serious. Brunson scored five of his eight points in the stretch during an 11–0 run that tied the tilt at 69, while the visitors blanked on eight consecutive attempts. Towns helped fuel the run by setting up Brunson and Shamet for buckets and blocking Watson at the cup. Hart later found McBride for another tying three at 74. Cleveland closed the quarter on an 8–2 run to take an 82–76 advantage into Q4.

Rough stretch for Bridges. He sat at the eight-minute mark of the third and came back with under two minutes left in the quarter. Allen blocked him on a layup, then took the ball away. Somehow, New York had attempted just five free throws through 40 minutes, all by Towns. The Cavs had taken 19 by then, eight by Harden alone.

Deuce scored the first five points of the fourth to pull the Knicks within one, but Mitchell answered with two layups, the second an and-one, and Proctor capped a 7–0 Cleveland run. Spida had two turnovers that led to McBride baskets, but he also set up Maleek Thomas for two buckets. With Brunson on the bench, McBride and Kolek ran the backcourt. Kolek fed Shamet for a three and KAT for a dunk that cut the deficit to seven with 7:35 left. Anunoby went on a tear with two freebies, a longball, a steal, and a breakaway feed to Hart for a bunny. Tie score at 99 with 5:36 to go.

Out of a timeout, Harden, Mobley, and Brunson scored to make it 106–103 with 2:18 on the clock. The game was still within reach, but Drummond fouled Mitchell and Allen scored four straight points, capitalizing on Brunson’s long brick. The deficit reached five with a minute to go. Brunson missed on a contested drive, Watson blocked McBride from behind on the fast break, and Harden hit his free throws. Ball game.

A Cup game in Indiana on Friday. Mo is tightening the bolts on his recap. Safe travels, Knickerbockers.
